lessons.title: Agriculture and national development
lessons.content:
# Agriculture and national development

Agriculture contributes to national development by supplying food, creating employment, and providing raw materials for processing industries. Farmers, transporters, market sellers, equipment makers, and food processors all take part in the agricultural economy. Selling products locally or abroad can bring income to households and revenue to businesses.

Reliable food production supports food security, but increasing output alone is not enough. Poor soil management, unsafe chemical use, and losses after harvest can harm communities and reduce long-term production. Investment in roads, storage, research, training, and fair markets can help farmers reach buyers and improve productivity.

When studying agriculture's contribution, consider who earns income, who receives food, and how resources are managed. Rural development is stronger when farming opportunities are paired with education, services, and protection of land and water.

Agriculture contributes to national development by supplying food and raw materials, creating work, supporting trade and earning income for households and businesses. Its effects extend beyond the farm: transporters move produce, processors add value, markets connect sellers with buyers, and banks or extension services help producers plan. Reliable local food production can also reduce dependence on imports, although trade remains important for foods and materials that cannot be produced efficiently in every region. For example, cassava may pass from a grower to a garri processor, a wholesaler and a market trader before reaching a household. Each stage adds work and cost. Development depends not only on harvest size but also on fair prices, storage, roads, soil care and access to useful knowledge.

lessons.title: Branches of agriculture
lessons.content:
# Branches of agriculture

Agriculture includes more than growing crops. Crop production concerns planting and harvesting food or fibre plants. Animal husbandry covers care and breeding of livestock. Fisheries deals with fish and other aquatic food; forestry manages trees and forest products. Agricultural engineering develops and maintains tools, machines, irrigation, and storage systems. Agricultural economics studies costs, markets, and decisions about farm resources.

These branches depend on one another. A crop farmer may use machinery, sell through a market, and keep livestock manure for soil improvement. Some farms specialise in one activity, while others combine several to reduce risk or use resources efficiently.

When comparing branches, identify their main products, skills, and resource needs. Their effects also matter: a farming method should be judged by output, cost, worker safety, and its impact on soil, water, and habitats.

The branches of agriculture are connected but require different knowledge. Crop production concerns establishing and managing plants; animal production covers the care and breeding of livestock; agricultural engineering applies tools, machinery and structures; agricultural economics studies costs, markets and farm decisions; and agricultural extension helps farmers learn and share improved practices. Soil science and forestry also support production and resource management. A mixed farm may grow maize for feed, keep poultry and use crop residues as bedding or compost. This example crosses several branches rather than fitting into one box. Knowing the branches helps a learner identify which specialist, tool or information source could help with a particular farm problem.

lessons.title: Farm planning
lessons.content:
# Farm planning

Farm planning means deciding what to produce, where and when to produce it, and which resources are available. A farmer considers soil, water, climate, land size, labour, tools, seed or livestock, expected costs, and access to buyers. A plan that ignores the rainy season or the distance to market may fail even when the crop is suitable.

A simple plan can list activities by date: prepare the land, obtain seed, plant, weed, monitor pests, harvest, and store or sell the crop. Budgeting estimates costs and likely income. Rotating crops can help manage soil nutrients and break some pest cycles; the choice must suit local conditions.

Plans should be reviewed as conditions change. A late rain or a damaged tool may require a new schedule. Keeping a record of what changed helps improve the next season's decisions.

A farm plan turns a production goal into a sequence of workable decisions. Before planting, the farmer considers land area, soil and water, crop variety, season, seed quantity, labour, tools, costs, likely buyers and possible risks. A simple field sketch can show beds, paths, water points and boundaries. If a plot is 20 metres by 10 metres, its area is 200 square metres; row spacing and paths determine how much is actually planted. A plan should include a calendar for land preparation, sowing, weeding and harvesting, as well as a budget and contingency for delayed rain or pests. Review the plan when conditions change. Planning does not guarantee success, but it exposes missing resources before they become costly problems.

lessons.title: Soil formation
lessons.content:
# Soil formation

Soil forms slowly as rock is broken into smaller particles by weathering and mixed with decayed plant and animal material. Rain, heat, wind, roots, and soil organisms contribute to this process. The original rock supplies mineral particles; humus from decomposed organic matter adds nutrients and helps soil hold water.

Climate affects how quickly weathering occurs, while slope influences whether soil stays in place or erodes. Over time, layers called horizons may develop. The upper layer often contains more organic material and supports many roots and organisms; lower layers can contain less humus and more weathered parent material.

Soil is not made in one season. Removing vegetation or exposing a slope can carry away fertile topsoil faster than natural processes replace it. Ground cover and careful water management help protect this slowly formed resource.

Soil forms slowly as parent rock breaks into smaller particles through heat, water, wind and living organisms. Plant roots and burrowing animals help loosen material; decaying leaves and other organic matter add humus. Climate affects how quickly rock weathers and how much material is washed or leached. Slope matters too: water can carry topsoil downhill, while flatter land may retain more material. Over time, layers called horizons develop. The upper topsoil often contains the most organic matter and many roots; lower layers contain more weathered material and parent rock. Digging a small profile at different depths can reveal changes in colour, texture and roots. Because fertile topsoil may take a long time to replace, erosion prevention and careful land use are essential.

lessons.title: Soil properties
lessons.content:
# Soil properties

Soil properties influence which crops can grow and how roots obtain water and air. Texture describes the relative amounts of sand, silt, and clay. Sandy soil drains quickly but may dry out; clay soil holds water and nutrients but can become waterlogged or hard when compacted. Loam contains a useful balance for many crops, though no soil type is ideal for every plant.

Structure describes how particles form aggregates. Good structure leaves spaces for roots, air, and water. Colour can offer clues about organic matter or drainage, but it does not prove fertility by itself. Acidity is measured by pH and affects nutrient availability.

Compare soil by examining a small, safely collected sample and recording texture, moisture, and drainage. A laboratory or approved test is needed for reliable nutrient or pH measurements before major farm decisions.

Soil properties influence which crops can grow and how water and nutrients behave. Texture describes the relative amounts of sand, silt and clay. Sandy soil drains quickly but may lose nutrients; clay holds water and nutrients but can become poorly drained; loam contains a useful balance for many crops. Structure describes how particles form aggregates, while porosity concerns the spaces that hold air and water. Soil pH affects nutrient availability and is measured with a suitable test. A simple hand test can compare how soil feels when moist, but it cannot replace a proper test. Observe drainage after rain, check for crusting and note the depth of roots. Match crop choice and soil improvement to measured conditions rather than judging soil by colour alone.

lessons.title: Soil sampling and testing
lessons.content:
# Soil sampling and testing

Soil sampling collects a small amount of soil that represents a larger field. A result is useful only if the sample reflects the area being tested. Divide a varied field into similar sections, avoid unusual spots such as manure heaps or paths, and collect several small samples from the same depth within each section.

Use a clean tool, remove surface litter, and place the subsamples for one section in a clean container. Mix them and label the sample with the field, date, and depth. Follow the instructions of the testing service; do not combine soil from different fields if their conditions differ.

A soil test may measure pH or nutrient levels and help guide fertiliser choices. It does not replace observation of crops or local advice. Keep chemicals and contaminated tools away from samples so the result is not distorted.

A soil test is only useful when the sample represents the field. Divide a large or visibly variable farm into management areas, then collect several small samples in a zigzag pattern from the same depth. Avoid unusual spots such as manure heaps, paths, burned areas or places beside a drain unless that location is the specific subject of the test. Remove surface litter, mix the subsamples in a clean container and place the composite sample in a labelled bag. Record the field, date, depth and recent fertilizer or lime use. A laboratory may test pH and nutrient levels and provide recommendations. Do not mix samples from different fields or depths, because the combined result can conceal a problem. Follow the sampling instructions of the service that will analyse the soil.

lessons.title: Soil fertility
lessons.content:
# Soil fertility

Soil fertility is the soil's ability to supply plants with the nutrients and conditions needed for healthy growth. Plants require nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, as well as water, air, and suitable root space. A crop may grow poorly because of drought, pests, or compacted soil even when nutrients are present.

Organic matter from compost or decomposed residues can improve soil structure and contribute nutrients. Fertilisers supply specific nutrients, but the correct type and amount depend on the crop and soil. Excess fertiliser can damage plants and pollute streams through runoff. Soil testing and local agricultural advice reduce guesswork.

Crop rotation, mulching, and preventing erosion help maintain productive soil. Fertility is not simply “add more fertiliser”; it requires matching soil care to crop needs and protecting the resource over time.

Soil fertility is the soil's capacity to supply nutrients in forms plants can use. Nitrogen supports leafy growth, phosphorus is important in energy transfer and root development, and potassium supports several plant functions, but crops also need secondary nutrients and trace elements. Organic matter improves soil structure and helps retain water and nutrients. Compost and well-managed manure can add organic matter; fertilizers supply nutrients in specified amounts. Neither should be applied blindly. A soil test, crop need, product label and recommended rate guide the choice. Too much fertilizer can damage plants, waste money or pollute waterways through runoff. Rotate crops, return suitable residues and protect soil from erosion. Fertility management combines nutrient supply with soil health rather than relying on one product.

lessons.title: Farm tools
lessons.content:
# Farm tools

Farm tools help with tasks such as clearing, digging, planting, weeding, and harvesting. A cutlass can clear light vegetation, a hoe loosens soil and removes weeds, a rake levels soil or gathers debris, and a spade turns or moves soil. The right tool depends on the task, soil, and user's strength; machines are used for larger jobs when available.

Inspect tools before use. A loose handle or cracked blade can cause injury. Carry sharp tools with the cutting edge pointed down and away from people, use them only for their intended purpose, and keep a safe distance from others. Wear sturdy footwear and other protection required for the activity.

After work, clean tools, dry metal parts, and store them safely. Regular care prevents rust and makes tools last longer. Never leave a blade hidden in grass or on a path.

Farm tools are selected for the job, soil condition and scale of work. A hoe can loosen soil and control small weeds; a cutlass can clear light vegetation; a rake levels soil or gathers debris; a watering can applies water to a small bed. Use each tool as designed and keep its handle, blade and fasteners in safe condition. A blunt or loose tool may require more force and can slip. After work, clean off soil, dry metal parts and store tools where children cannot trip over or handle them unsupervised. Carry sharp tools with the cutting edge controlled and pointed away from people. For larger tasks, a wheelbarrow or suitable machine may save effort, but only trained users should operate powered equipment. Maintenance extends tool life and reduces avoidable injuries.

lessons.title: Farm safety
lessons.content:
# Farm safety

Farm safety means preventing injury to workers, visitors, animals, and the environment. Common hazards include sharp tools, moving equipment, chemicals, uneven ground, heat, and animals that may kick or bite. Before starting a task, identify the hazard and follow the instructions of a trained adult or supervisor.

Wear suitable footwear and protective clothing. Keep children away from machinery, store chemicals in labelled containers away from food, and never mix or apply pesticides without proper training and protective equipment. Wash hands after handling soil, animals, or farm products. Drink safe water and take breaks in hot weather.

Know how to call for help and where first-aid supplies are kept. Do not attempt a task beyond your training. Reporting a near miss can prevent a more serious accident later.

Farm work can involve sharp tools, animals, chemicals, machinery, heat and uneven ground. Before starting, identify hazards, agree on safe movement and keep bystanders away from work areas. Wear suitable footwear and protective clothing; gloves and eye protection are needed for particular tasks, but must be appropriate to the tool or substance. Read pesticide labels, keep chemicals in their original labelled containers and never transfer them to drink bottles. Store chemicals away from food, water and children. Know where first-aid supplies and emergency contacts are kept. Stop work if equipment is damaged or conditions become unsafe, and tell the responsible adult or supervisor.

lessons.title: Crop classification
lessons.content:
# Crop classification

Crops can be grouped by the products people use. Cereals such as maize and rice provide grain; legumes such as beans can provide protein and enrich soil through nitrogen-fixing bacteria; roots and tubers such as cassava and yam store food below ground. Oil crops, vegetables, fruits, and fibre crops each serve different needs.

Crops can also be classified by life cycle. Annual crops complete their life cycle in one growing season, biennials take two seasons, and perennials live for several years. The same crop may belong to more than one category: a crop can be both a legume and an annual.

Classification helps farmers plan spacing, harvesting, storage, and crop rotation. When sorting examples, state the basis of the group—use, plant part, or life cycle—so different categories are not confused.

Crops can be grouped by their use, life cycle or plant family. Cereals such as maize and rice are grown mainly for grain; legumes such as beans and groundnuts produce pods and can contribute nitrogen through root-associated bacteria; roots and tubers include cassava, yam and sweet potato; vegetables and fruits are grown for edible leaves, stems, roots or fruits. Some crops have more than one use. Classification helps farmers plan rotations, storage and marketing. For example, alternating maize with a suitable legume can break some pest cycles and improve soil nitrogen when residues are managed well. A crop's group does not replace checking its exact water, soil, temperature and planting requirements. Use the intended product and growth habit to classify unfamiliar crops, then consult reliable guidance before choosing a production method.

lessons.title: Seed selection
lessons.content:
# Seed selection

Good seed should be mature, healthy, viable, and suitable for the local climate and soil. Seed from a reliable source is more likely to have the expected variety and germination rate. Avoid seed that is mouldy, damaged, shrivelled, or mixed with stones and other seeds. A large seed is not automatically better; health and suitability matter more than size alone.

A simple germination test can estimate how many seeds will sprout. Place a known number between moist paper or cloth, keep it warm, and count the seeds that germinate after the recommended time. If 8 of 10 sprout, the test suggests an 80 percent germination rate.

Store seed in a labelled, dry, cool place, protected from pests. Keep varieties separate and record the date. Seed treated with chemicals must be handled only as its label directs and never eaten.

Good seed should match the local climate, soil, growing season and intended market. Farmers consider variety, purity, viability, maturity period and resistance to common pests or disease. Certified seed usually comes with information about its identity and quality, while saved seed should be selected from healthy, true-to-type plants and stored dry and safely. A small germination test can estimate viability: place a known number of seeds in a moist medium under suitable conditions and count how many sprout. If 18 of 20 seeds germinate, the observed germination is 90 percent. That result can help adjust the sowing rate, but field conditions may differ from the test. Do not use mouldy, damaged or mixed seed. Keep labels and note the source and date so performance can be compared after harvest.

lessons.title: Planting methods
lessons.content:
# Planting methods

Planting method affects spacing, seed use, and early growth. Broadcasting scatters seed over a prepared area and is useful for some small seeds, but plants may emerge unevenly. Drilling places seed in rows at a controlled depth and spacing. Dibbling places individual seeds in holes, which can suit larger seeds or small plots.

The correct depth depends on seed size and soil moisture. Planting too deeply can prevent a small seedling from reaching the surface; planting too shallowly may leave seed exposed to drying or birds. Follow recommendations for the crop and keep rows straight enough for weeding and later care.

Before planting, check the seed rate, spacing, season, and soil condition. Label a small trial row and observe emergence; this helps identify whether poor growth is due to seed, depth, water, or another factor.

Planting method depends on the crop, seed size, soil moisture and available equipment. Direct sowing places seed in its final growing position; transplanting raises seedlings in a nursery and moves them later. Broadcasting spreads seed over a surface, while drilling or dibbling places it at planned spacing and depth. Correct depth protects seed and allows the shoot to emerge; planting too deep can exhaust a small seed's reserves, while shallow seed may dry out or be eaten. Spacing reduces competition and allows access for weeding and harvesting. For example, a row plan for maize should follow the recommended spacing for the variety and local conditions rather than a guessed distance. Water after planting when needed, but avoid flooding. Record the date, method and seed source for later comparison.

lessons.title: Crop maintenance
lessons.content:
# Crop maintenance

After planting, crops need regular observation and care. Weeding reduces competition for light, water, and nutrients. Thinning removes extra seedlings so the remaining plants have enough space. Mulch can conserve moisture and limit some weeds; irrigation supplies water when rainfall is insufficient.

Some crops need staking or pruning, while others need fertiliser based on soil and crop requirements. Inspect leaves and stems for signs of pests, disease, or nutrient stress. Do not treat every damaged leaf with chemicals: first identify the cause and consider safe, approved controls.

Maintenance should protect both the crop and the soil. Avoid working wet soil when it would compact, and prevent runoff from carrying fertiliser into drains or streams. Keeping dates and observations in a farm record helps compare methods and improve future crops.

Crop maintenance supports healthy growth after establishment. It can include watering, gap filling, thinning, mulching, staking, weeding, nutrient management and regular inspection. The right action depends on the crop and its growth stage. Thinning removes excess seedlings so remaining plants have enough light, water and nutrients; gap filling replaces failed plants while nearby plants are still young. Mulch can reduce evaporation and suppress weeds, but contaminated or diseased material should not be spread. Water at a time that reduces evaporation and avoid waterlogging roots. Inspect leaves and stems for changes, then identify the cause before applying a treatment. Keep a record of what was done and when. A maintenance plan should balance crop needs, labour and water availability, not follow a calendar blindly when weather or plant condition calls for adjustment.

lessons.title: Weeds and weed control
lessons.content:
# Weeds and weed control

A weed is a plant growing where it is unwanted. Weeds compete with crops for light, water, space, and nutrients; some also shelter pests. Identify the weed before choosing a control method because annual weeds and deep-rooted perennials may respond differently.

Control methods include hand pulling, hoeing, mulching, crop rotation, and planting crops closely enough to shade the soil. Remove weeds before they set seed when practical. A weed with underground stems may regrow if only its leaves are cut, so follow safe, locally advised methods.

Herbicides can harm people, useful plants, and water if misused. Only trained adults should select and apply an approved product according to its label and protective requirements. Monitoring the field and combining suitable methods is safer and more effective than relying on one treatment.

Weeds compete with crops for light, water, nutrients and space. Some also shelter pests or interfere with harvesting. Control begins with identification and prevention: clean seed, clean tools and well-managed field edges can reduce weed spread. Hand weeding or hoeing is suitable for small areas when the crop can be protected; mulching blocks light from reaching many weed seedlings. Crop rotation and close crop spacing can also suppress some weeds. Herbicides should only be used when appropriate, by trained people following the product label and protective requirements. Spraying the wrong product or applying it in wind can injure crops, people or nearby plants. Remove weeds before they set seed when possible, and dispose of invasive or diseased plants safely. Choose an approach based on weed type, crop stage, field size and environmental risk.

lessons.title: Pests and diseases
lessons.content:
# Pests and diseases

A pest is an organism that damages crops or competes with them; a disease is a harmful condition often caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses, or other pathogens. Chewed leaves may suggest an insect pest, while spots, wilting, or rotting can have several causes. Symptoms alone do not always identify the problem, so inspect carefully or ask an agricultural extension worker.

Integrated pest management combines methods: use healthy seed, rotate crops, remove infected material safely, encourage helpful organisms, and monitor fields. A pesticide should be considered only when appropriate, approved for the crop, and applied by a trained person following the label.

Never touch, taste, or spray an unknown substance. Keep people, animals, and water sources protected. Early identification and accurate records can reduce crop loss without unnecessary chemical use.

Crop pests damage plants by feeding, boring or transmitting disease; diseases may be caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses or other organisms. Look for patterns such as holes, discolouration, wilting or unusual growth, and check several plants before deciding what is wrong. Nutrient deficiency, drought and waterlogging can resemble disease, so identification matters. Integrated pest management combines prevention, monitoring, cultural practices, biological control and carefully chosen pesticides when needed. Crop rotation, resistant varieties, clean tools and removal of infected material can reduce risk. If treatment is necessary, use a product labelled for that crop and pest, follow dosage and re-entry instructions, wear required protection and avoid spraying near water or pollinators. Keep a record of symptoms, weather and actions. Treating every symptom with chemicals can waste money and harm beneficial organisms.

lessons.title: Harvesting and storage
lessons.content:
# Harvesting and storage

Harvest crops when they are mature enough for their intended use. The signs differ: grain may become dry and firm, while vegetables may be picked at a tender stage. Harvesting too early can reduce quality; delay can expose produce to rain, pests, or spoilage. Use clean tools and handle produce carefully to avoid cuts and bruising.

After harvest, sort out damaged or diseased items. Dry grains to a safe moisture level before storage, and keep them in clean, dry containers protected from insects and rodents. Fresh produce may need shade, ventilation, cooling, or quick transport to market. Storage methods depend on the crop.

Good post-harvest handling preserves food and income. Record the quantity harvested and any losses; this can show whether a change in timing or storage would help next season.

Harvest at the stage that suits the crop's intended use. Immature produce may have poor flavour or low weight, while overripe produce can soften, split or attract pests. Use clean tools and containers, avoid dropping or bruising produce and keep harvested crops out of direct sun when appropriate. Grain must be dried to a safe moisture level before storage; damp grain can mould or heat. Store products in clean, dry, pest-resistant containers and inspect them regularly. Separate damaged or diseased items so they do not spoil sound produce. For example, drying maize before placing it in a sealed store helps reduce mould risk, but it should be dried and handled safely. Record quantity, date and storage condition. Good post-harvest handling preserves quality and income, though no method removes the need to monitor stored produce.

lessons.title: Livestock classification
lessons.content:
# Livestock classification

Livestock are domesticated animals raised for products or services. Cattle, sheep, and goats are ruminants: their digestive systems allow them to digest fibrous feed through fermentation. Pigs are non-ruminants, and poultry such as chickens are birds with different feeding and housing needs. Fish are raised in aquaculture systems rather than on land.

Animals can also be grouped by their main products: milk, meat, eggs, hides, or work. One species may provide more than one product; cattle can supply milk, meat, and hides. Classification is useful because housing, feed, health care, and handling differ by species and purpose.

When comparing livestock, identify their features and needs rather than assuming one care method fits all. Any handling should be calm and supervised to protect both people and animals.

Livestock can be classified by species, use, feeding system or digestive system. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants with a multi-compartment stomach that supports digestion of fibrous feeds; pigs are monogastric; poultry have a different digestive system and are kept for meat or eggs. Animals may also be grouped as dairy, meat, draft or dual-purpose breeds, but actual performance depends on breed, health, feed and management. Classification helps farmers choose housing, nutrition and breeding practices. For example, a dairy cow needs a routine that supports milk production and udder health, while broilers are managed for efficient meat growth. Do not assume every animal of a named breed has the same output. Identify the production goal and local suitability before choosing stock, and obtain animals from a healthy, reliable source.

lessons.title: Animal housing
lessons.content:
# Animal housing

Animal housing protects livestock from extreme weather, predators, and injury while making feeding and cleaning manageable. A suitable shelter needs enough space for the species and number of animals, ventilation, shade, drainage, and access to clean water. Overcrowding can increase stress and allow disease to spread more easily.

Housing must match animal behaviour. Poultry need secure night shelter and clean litter; goats need dry space and strong fencing; fish need a pond or tank with suitable water quality. Floors should be kept clean without allowing waste to contaminate water sources.

Inspect shelters regularly for broken fencing, leaks, sharp edges, and signs of illness. Separate a sick animal only with guidance from a knowledgeable adult or animal-health worker. Good housing supports welfare as well as farm productivity.

Animal housing protects livestock from extreme weather, predators, injury and disease while allowing suitable movement and ventilation. Housing needs differ by species and age. Poultry houses require dry litter, airflow and enough floor space; goat pens need secure fencing and a raised, dry resting area; fish ponds require managed water quality rather than a building. Clean manure and soiled bedding regularly, provide clean water and separate sick animals when advised. Overcrowding raises stress and disease risk, while poor ventilation allows moisture and harmful gases to build up. A housing plan should include drainage, feeding and watering points, safe access for workers and a method for cleaning. Inspect structures for sharp edges, broken wire and leaks. Good housing is not simply shelter; it is part of daily health management and should be adapted to local climate and available materials.

lessons.title: Animal nutrition
lessons.content:
# Animal nutrition

Animals need energy, protein, vitamins, minerals, and clean water. The right balance depends on the species, age, size, and whether the animal is growing, laying eggs, producing milk, or doing work. Roughage such as grass supplies fibre for ruminants; concentrates provide more energy or protein in a smaller quantity.

A balanced ration supplies needed nutrients without waste. Moldy or spoiled feed can harm animals and should not be given. Introduce feed changes gradually, provide clean water every day, and store feed where it stays dry and protected from pests.

Observe appetite, body condition, and growth. A sudden change may indicate illness, poor feed, or water problems. Seek advice before using supplements or medicines; correct nutrition supports health but does not replace veterinary care.

Animals need energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and clean water in amounts that depend on species, age, body condition and production. Roughage such as pasture supplies fibre for ruminants; concentrates provide denser energy or protein. Poultry and pigs need balanced formulated feeds because their digestive systems and growth targets differ. Feed changes should be gradual to reduce digestive upset. Observe appetite, body condition, growth, egg production or milk output as signs of whether management is working, but seek qualified advice when animals become ill. Store feed dry and protected from rodents, mould and chemicals. Do not feed spoiled or unknown plants. A ration should use safe local ingredients and meet animal requirements rather than rely on one ingredient. Clean water is essential; poor water access can reduce feed intake and production even when feed is adequate.

lessons.title: Poultry production
lessons.content:
# Poultry production

Poultry production raises birds such as chickens, ducks, or turkeys for eggs or meat. Layers are managed for egg production; broilers are selected for meat growth. Birds need suitable housing, clean water, balanced feed, and protection from predators and disease. Chicks require warmth and careful monitoring when young.

Keep drinkers and feeders clean, provide enough space, and remove wet litter so harmful organisms do not build up. New or sick birds should be handled according to guidance from an animal-health worker. Vaccination and disease-control schedules should follow local veterinary advice.

Farmers record the number of birds, feed used, eggs collected, deaths, and sales. These records help detect a problem early and calculate whether the enterprise is covering its costs. People handling birds should wash their hands afterward.

Poultry production includes raising chickens and other domestic birds for eggs, meat or breeding. A flock needs suitable housing, clean water, balanced feed, appropriate temperature and a vaccination and biosecurity plan guided by local veterinary advice. Broilers are selected for meat production and layers for egg production; their housing and feeding programmes differ. Start with healthy chicks from a reliable source and keep age groups separate where possible. Clean equipment between batches, restrict unnecessary visitors and remove dead birds safely according to local guidance. Record feed use, mortality, egg numbers or weight gain so changes can be noticed early. A sudden drop in feed intake or egg production can signal heat stress, disease or a water problem. Do not treat every problem with medicine without diagnosis; prevention and prompt professional advice protect the flock and consumers.

lessons.title: Fish farming
lessons.content:
# Fish farming

Fish farming, or aquaculture, raises fish in ponds, tanks, or other managed water systems. Success depends on suitable water quality, healthy fingerlings, appropriate stocking density, adequate feed, and protection from predators. Too many fish in a small pond can reduce oxygen and increase disease risk.

Check water for unusual colour, smell, temperature changes, and fish behaviour such as gasping at the surface. These signs may indicate poor water conditions, but ask an experienced fish farmer or extension worker before taking corrective action. Feed only the amount fish can consume; uneaten feed pollutes the water and wastes money.

Harvest at the size and time suited to the market. Keep equipment clean and prevent farmed fish or waste from damaging nearby water bodies. Record stocking, feed, growth, losses, and sales.

Fish farming raises fish in ponds, tanks or other managed systems. Success depends on suitable species, clean water, adequate dissolved oxygen, appropriate stocking density and feed. Pond preparation may include repairing leaks, clearing unwanted organisms and checking water conditions before stocking. Fingerlings should be active and similar in size; mixing very different sizes can increase competition or cannibalism in some species. Feed small amounts at regular times and observe whether fish consume it. Uneaten feed decomposes, lowers water quality and wastes money. Check water colour, smell, fish behaviour and water level, and seek technical help if fish gasp at the surface or die unexpectedly. Keep records of stocking, feeding, growth, water changes and harvest. Fish farming is a managed production system, not simply placing fish in water and waiting.

lessons.title: Goat and sheep production
lessons.content:
# Goat and sheep production

Goats and sheep are ruminants: they digest fibrous plants through a stomach system that includes fermentation. Goats often browse leaves and shrubs, while sheep commonly graze grasses, though both need feed suited to their health and local conditions. Clean water, adequate space, and nutritious forage are essential.

Provide a dry, ventilated shelter with secure fencing to protect animals from weather, theft, and predators. Keep the area clean and separate feed from waste. Observe appetite, movement, and body condition; signs of illness should be discussed with an animal-health worker rather than treated by guesswork.

Farmers may raise them for meat, milk, skins, or breeding stock. Records of births, feed, health care, deaths, and sales help plan the herd and calculate costs. Calm handling protects both the animals and the people caring for them.

Goats and sheep are ruminants raised for meat, milk, fibre, breeding or a combination of uses. Their management includes choosing healthy stock, providing dry shelter, suitable forage, clean water and routine health care. Goats often browse shrubs and leaves, while sheep generally graze grasses, but feeding varies by breed and available pasture. A balanced diet may need supplements during pregnancy, lactation or rapid growth. Inspect hooves, body condition and signs of parasites, and ask a trained animal-health worker about vaccination and treatment schedules. Keep young animals safe from cold, wet conditions and predators. Record births, parentage, treatments and sales to track flock performance. Avoid buying animals without checking health and origin. Good management improves welfare and productivity while reducing preventable losses.

lessons.title: Farm records
lessons.content:
# Farm records

Farm records preserve information needed to plan and evaluate a farm. A crop record may include the variety planted, date, seed quantity, field, fertiliser, pest observations, harvest, and sales. Livestock records can track births, feed, health care, eggs or milk, deaths, and purchases.

Financial records list money received and spent, with dates and supporting receipts where available. Comparing costs with sales helps the farmer estimate profit or identify an expense that is rising. Records also help recall which seed or method performed well in a particular season.

Write entries promptly, use consistent units, and keep records in a safe place. A record is useful only if it is accurate and understandable. Do not change a figure to make a result look better; note a correction and keep the original information clear.

Farm records preserve information needed to manage production and money. Useful records include planting dates, seed varieties, fertilizer use, labour, feed, animal health, harvest quantities, sales and expenses. A record is most useful when entries are dated, legible and made consistently. For a crop plot, noting seed quantity, rainfall, weeding dates and harvest weight can help compare varieties or methods in the next season. Separate estimates from measured values and keep receipts where possible. Records can reveal that a field yields less, that feed costs are rising or that a product sells well only at certain times. Protect private financial information and keep copies in a safe place. Records do not make a farm successful by themselves, but they support evidence-based decisions and help farmers explain costs, apply for support or plan future production.

lessons.title: Marketing farm products
lessons.content:
# Marketing farm products

Marketing connects farm products with buyers. Farmers may sell directly, through a cooperative, to a trader, or through a processor. The best route depends on the amount produced, distance, storage life, transport cost, and price offered. A higher market price may not mean greater profit if transport and handling costs are also high.

Sorting and grading group products by size or quality so buyers know what they are purchasing. Clean packaging and careful handling can prevent damage, while storage may allow a farmer to wait for a suitable market. Perishable crops often need quick sale or processing.

Before agreeing to sell, compare prices, measure costs, and confirm the quantity and payment terms. Keeping records of buyers and sales helps farmers plan production and avoid relying on memory.

Marketing farm products connects producers with buyers. It includes understanding demand, grading quality, packaging, setting prices, choosing a market, transporting goods and communicating availability. A farmer compares the expected selling price with production and marketing costs. Selling at the farm gate may reduce transport work but often offers a different price from selling in a town market. Perishable goods need quick handling and an agreed buyer. Weigh products accurately, use clean packaging and state the variety or grade honestly. Check local market prices across several days because prices can change with supply, season and transport conditions. A cooperative can help farmers bulk produce or negotiate, but members need clear records and agreed rules. Marketing is more than advertising; it includes delivering the right product, in good condition, where and when customers need it.

lessons.title: Agricultural extension
lessons.content:
# Agricultural extension

Agricultural extension links farmers with practical information, training, and services that may improve production and livelihoods. Extension workers can explain a new crop variety, demonstrate safe equipment use, or help diagnose a field problem. Effective extension is a two-way exchange: farmers share their experience and constraints, not just receive instructions.

A demonstration plot can compare two planting methods under similar conditions. Farmers observe the results and discuss costs, labour, and suitability for their own land. A method that works in one location may not work elsewhere because soils, rainfall, and resources differ.

Reliable advice should be checked against local conditions and evidence. Farmers can keep notes from a trial and consult qualified agricultural services before changing a whole farm. Extension supports informed decisions rather than guaranteeing a particular harvest.

Agricultural extension shares practical information between farmers, researchers, advisers and other rural organisations. Extension workers may demonstrate planting methods, explain pest monitoring, discuss animal health or connect farmers with soil testing and markets. Advice should fit local conditions and be clear about evidence and limitations. A demonstration plot can compare two varieties under the same management, but differences in soil or water between plots may affect the result. Farmers contribute local experience and should be able to ask questions or report outcomes. Before adopting a new practice, consider its cost, labour, safety, environmental effect and suitability for the farm. Extension is not simply telling farmers what to do; it is a two-way process that helps adapt useful knowledge and identify problems for further study.

lessons.title: Sustainable agriculture
lessons.content:
# Sustainable agriculture

Sustainable agriculture aims to produce food and income while maintaining the soil, water, biodiversity, and livelihoods that farming depends on. Practices can include crop rotation, cover crops, compost, efficient irrigation, and integrated pest management. The suitable combination depends on climate, land, labour, and available resources.

For example, rotating a cereal crop with a legume can vary nutrient demands and may improve soil nitrogen when the right legume and management are used. Mulching can reduce evaporation, but materials and pests must be managed. No single practice makes every farm sustainable by itself.

Farmers can track yields, soil condition, water use, and costs over several seasons. Comparing these measures helps reveal whether production is maintained without exhausting resources or creating avoidable harm for nearby communities.

Sustainable agriculture produces food and income while maintaining the soil, water, biodiversity and farm resources needed in the future. Practices may include crop rotation, cover crops, compost, careful water use, integrated pest management and reduced soil disturbance where appropriate. No single practice suits every farm, and the result depends on local soil, climate, labour and markets. For example, rotating a cereal with a legume can interrupt some pest cycles and improve nitrogen availability, but the farmer still needs to manage residues and plan the next crop. Avoid clearing steep slopes without protection, wasting irrigation water or applying chemicals without need. Evaluate sustainability over time by monitoring yield, soil condition, costs and environmental effects. A practice is not sustainable merely because it is traditional or labelled natural; assess its actual outcomes.

lessons.title: Farm enterprise project
lessons.content:
# Farm enterprise project

A farm enterprise project plans a small agricultural activity from idea to evaluation. Choose a realistic product, such as a short row of vegetables, and identify the land, seed, tools, water, labour, and permission required. Estimate costs before starting and decide who will perform each task.

Create a simple schedule for preparation, planting, maintenance, and harvest. Follow safety rules and keep a record of dates, materials used, problems, and output. If conditions change, note the change rather than hiding it. A small project should not use chemicals or equipment beyond the learners' training.

At the end, compare the harvest and costs with the original goal. Explain what worked, what did not, and what you would change next time. A project is valuable even when results are modest, provided the evidence is recorded honestly.

A farm enterprise project plans a small production activity from goal to evaluation. Choose a product suited to available land, season, water, skills and likely buyers. Estimate inputs such as seed, feed, tools, labour, transport and packaging. Set a calendar for each operation and identify risks such as pests, price changes, delayed rain or animal illness. Use a notebook to record actual spending, work completed, problems and harvest or sales. At the end, compare the result with the plan: calculate revenue and costs, note unsold or damaged products, and explain why outcomes differed from expectations. A project may be a school garden, a small poultry group or a supervised container crop. Follow safety rules and obtain permission before using land or animals. The report should state what the evidence shows and what should change next time.

lessons.title: Physical fitness
lessons.content:
# Physical fitness

## Fitness for everyday life

Physical fitness is the capacity to carry out ordinary work and physical activity without becoming exhausted too quickly. It is not the same as being an athlete, and it cannot be judged from appearance alone. A person may be strong but tire quickly when running; another may have good endurance but need to develop balance or flexibility. Fitness changes with practice, health, age and rest.

## Building it safely

Walking, active games, dancing and household tasks can all contribute to movement. Improvement comes from regular activity that is suitable for the person, followed by recovery. Start at a manageable pace, drink water, use safe space and stop if pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness occurs. A simple record of activity and how the body feels is more useful than comparing one learner's performance with another's.

Fitness develops through regular activity, suitable recovery and gradual progression. A learner beginning a walking routine should choose a comfortable pace, record duration and notice how the body responds rather than competing with a classmate. Sleep, hydration and rest support adaptation. Changes in performance can reflect illness, stress or conditions on the day, so compare records made in similar circumstances. Fitness is not a measure of a person's worth or appearance; it is one part of wellbeing and should be approached safely.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes physical fitness?
options: The ability to perform daily physical tasks effectively and recover appropriately
Winning every sporting event
Having a particular body shape
Training hard without rest

quiz.question: A learner feels dizzy during a run. What is the safest response?
options: Stop, move to a safe place and tell the teacher
Run faster to finish sooner
Ignore it if others are still running
Skip water for the rest of the day

lessons.activity: Keep a three-day activity record. Note the activity, its duration, how hard it felt, and one sign that you need rest or water.
commonMistakes: Fitness is not measured by body shape or by one event; different activities draw on different abilities.
lessons.summary: Physical fitness is the capacity to carry out ordinary work and physical activity without becoming exhausted too quickly. It is not the same as being an athlete, and it cannot be judged from appearance alone. A person may be strong but tire quickly when running; another may have good endurance but need to develop balan
lessons.objective: Explain physical fitness as a set of abilities that supports daily activity and identify safe ways to improve it.

lessons.title: Health-related fitness
lessons.content:
# Health-related fitness

## Fitness that supports health

Health-related fitness describes abilities that help the body function well in daily life. Its commonly taught components are cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. These are related but not interchangeable. The heart and lungs support sustained activity; muscles produce and repeat force; flexible joints move through a useful range. Body composition describes the proportions of tissues in the body and should not be used to shame or rank classmates.

## Readiness matters

An activity can develop more than one component. Brisk walking mainly challenges endurance, while a controlled wall push-up uses muscular strength and endurance. Progress should be gradual and appropriate to the learner. A fitness check is a way to notice change, not a diagnosis or competition. Compare a learner's current performance with their own earlier record, using the same safe procedure.

The health-related components describe different abilities, so an assessment should name the component it measures. A timed walk can provide information about cardiorespiratory endurance, while a controlled flexibility task assesses range of movement. Results depend on the protocol, effort, age and health, and should not be used to diagnose disease. Compare a learner's record over time using the same method and allow privacy. A balanced programme includes more than one component, with activities chosen to be accessible and enjoyable rather than focused on ranking pupils.

quiz.question: Which component is most directly challenged by a sustained brisk walk?
options: Cardiorespiratory endurance
Flexibility
Reaction time
Body composition alone

quiz.question: What is the best use of a repeated fitness check?
options: Compare progress using the same safe procedure
Diagnose a disease
Rank learners by body type
Replace advice from a health professional

lessons.activity: Choose two accessible activities and identify the health-related fitness component each is likely to develop, explaining your reasoning.
commonMistakes: A fitness test does not diagnose illness, and a single score does not describe a person's overall health.
lessons.summary: Health-related fitness describes abilities that help the body function well in daily life. Its commonly taught components are cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. These are related but not interchangeable. The heart and lungs support sustained activity; m
lessons.objective: Name the major health-related fitness components and distinguish a fitness check from a medical diagnosis.

lessons.title: Components of fitness
lessons.content:
# Components of fitness

## Different abilities, different demands

Health-related components include cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components include speed, agility, balance, coordination, power and reaction time. A sport rarely depends on only one. A footballer needs endurance to keep moving, agility to change direction, coordination to control the ball and strength to contest space safely.

## Make a fair comparison

Strength is the force a muscle can produce; muscular endurance is its ability to repeat or sustain work. Power combines force with speed. Speed is moving quickly, while agility is changing direction with control. Balance keeps the body stable; coordination links movements smoothly. These distinctions help a learner select suitable practice. They do not mean one component is more valuable in every sport or for every person.

Skill-related components such as balance, agility, coordination, power, reaction time and speed support particular movements, while health-related components support general function. A basketball player may need agility to change direction, but that does not make agility the only valuable ability. Match practice to the task and teach technique before increasing intensity. Observe movement quality and safety as well as time or distance. When comparing results, explain which component is being considered and avoid presenting one test as a complete picture of fitness.

quiz.question: A player changes direction quickly while staying in control. Which component is most evident?
options: Agility
Flexibility
Body composition
Static strength

quiz.question: Which statement distinguishes strength from muscular endurance?
options: Strength concerns force; endurance concerns sustaining or repeating effort
Strength is balance; endurance is reaction time
They mean exactly the same thing
Endurance is the fastest movement

lessons.activity: Select a sport and make a two-column chart: the movement demands you observe and the fitness components that support them.
commonMistakes: Speed, agility and power are related but have different meanings; do not use their names as if they were synonyms.
lessons.summary: Health-related components include cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components include speed, agility, balance, coordination, power and reaction time. A sport rarely depends on only one. A footballer needs endurance to keep moving, agilit
lessons.objective: Distinguish commonly confused fitness components and relate them to the demands of a sport.

lessons.title: Warm-up and cool-down
lessons.content:
# Warm-up and cool-down

## Prepare before vigorous movement

A warm-up moves the body gradually from rest toward the demands of exercise. It can begin with easy walking or jogging, followed by controlled movements that resemble the activity ahead. For a game involving changes of direction, learners might add gentle side steps and short accelerations after their pulse and breathing have begun to rise. A warm-up should not leave the class exhausted.

## Return to rest gradually

A cool-down reduces activity at a steady pace rather than stopping abruptly after hard exercise. Easy walking and calm breathing allow the body to settle. Gentle stretching may follow when muscles are warm; bouncing or forcing a stretch is not necessary. Neither routine guarantees that injury will never occur, but preparation, suitable technique, safe space and attention to discomfort all help reduce avoidable risk.

A warm-up should prepare the body for the activity that follows. Begin with light movement, then use controlled dynamic actions related to the session; a sprinter may include progressive running drills. A cool-down gradually reduces activity and can include gentle movement and reflection. Neither routine guarantees that injury will not occur, and stretching should not be forced through pain. Adjust the warm-up for weather, space and the learner's condition. Stop and tell the teacher if dizziness, chest discomfort or unusual pain occurs.

quiz.question: Why should a warm-up move from easy activity toward game-like movement?
options: It raises activity gradually and prepares the body for the task
It uses up energy before the game
It guarantees that no injury can happen
It replaces learning the rules

quiz.question: What is a suitable cool-down after vigorous activity?
options: Reduce effort gradually with easy movement
Sit down suddenly without checking how you feel
Sprint until completely exhausted
Force a stretch until it hurts

lessons.activity: Plan a five-minute warm-up for a chosen game. Put the activities in order from easiest to most like the game, and explain the progression.
commonMistakes: A warm-up is not a tiring workout, and stretching through sharp pain is not a safe preparation method.
lessons.summary: A warm-up moves the body gradually from rest toward the demands of exercise. It can begin with easy walking or jogging, followed by controlled movements that resemble the activity ahead. For a game involving changes of direction, learners might add gentle side steps and short accelerations after their pulse and breathi
lessons.objective: Describe how a progressive warm-up and cool-down prepare for and end physical activity.

lessons.title: Athletics
lessons.content:
# Athletics

## A family of track and field events

Athletics includes running, jumping and throwing events. Track events use marked lanes or routes; field events take place in a designated area. Each event has its own technique and rules, but all require preparation, attention to instructions and respect for other competitors. The event is not simply a test of effort: a legal attempt must follow the rules for the start, route, landing area or implement.

## Organise a safe event

Before practice, inspect the surface and equipment, mark boundaries, and make sure participants know when to begin and where to wait. In throwing events, only the thrower enters the throwing area, and everyone retrieves an implement after the teacher's signal. In jumping events, the landing area must be clear. Officials apply the same rules to each competitor and record attempts consistently.

Athletics combines events that test running, jumping and throwing, each with its own techniques and safety requirements. Before practice, inspect the surface, mark clear lanes and keep spectators outside the event area. Learners should understand where equipment will travel and wait for an official signal before retrieving it. Performance records are useful only when conditions and rules are comparable. Teach the movement in manageable stages, give specific feedback and allow rest. Participation can be adapted so that learners with different abilities practise meaningfully without creating unsafe competition.

quiz.question: Which pair contains one track event and one field event?
options: A 100-metre race and a long jump
A relay and a sprint
A high jump and a shot put
A discus throw and a javelin throw

quiz.question: When should a class retrieve a thrown implement?
options: After the teacher or official gives the signal
While another learner is preparing to throw
Whenever a learner wants to
Before the attempt is recorded

lessons.activity: Sort a list of school events into track and field categories, then write one safety check for each category.
commonMistakes: Athletics is broader than running; jumping and throwing are also field events with distinct safety rules.
lessons.summary: Athletics includes running, jumping and throwing events. Track events use marked lanes or routes; field events take place in a designated area. Each event has its own technique and rules, but all require preparation, attention to instructions and respect for other competitors. The event is not simply a test of effort:
lessons.objective: Classify athletics events and explain how event rules and safe organisation protect participants.

lessons.title: Running events
lessons.content:
# Running events

## Distance changes the race plan

Sprints, middle-distance races, long-distance races and relays place different demands on runners. A sprint requires a controlled start and rapid acceleration. Longer races require a pace the runner can maintain; starting too fast can leave little energy for the finish. Relay teams add baton exchange, timing and communication. In every race, runners must follow the start signal and remain within the rules for their event.

## Practise with control

Use a clear, even surface and leave space beyond the finish so runners can slow down safely. Warm up before fast running, wear suitable footwear and do not cross another runner's lane. A teacher can help learners compare pacing by recording split times over equal sections. The aim is to understand effort and technique, not to push through pain or compete while unwell.

Running technique depends on the event. A short sprint emphasises a controlled start, acceleration and maintaining form, while distance running requires an even pace and judgement about effort. Learners should warm up, run in the correct direction and avoid crossing another runner's lane. Record distance and time with a consistent method, then use the result to plan gradual improvement. A fast first lap followed by exhaustion may indicate poor pacing. Stop if a learner feels unwell, and do not use performance comparisons to shame or pressure anyone.

quiz.question: What is a sensible pacing choice for a long-distance race?
options: Choose an effort that can be maintained across the distance
Sprint at maximum speed from the first step
Copy another runner without noticing your own condition
Ignore the route and start signal

quiz.question: What must relay teammates coordinate?
options: The timing and legal exchange of the baton
The removal of lane markings
The order in which spectators run
A finish before the start signal

lessons.activity: Record two equal sections of a comfortable run. Compare the times and describe whether your pace stayed steady.
commonMistakes: A distance runner does not need to sprint every section; pace should match the event and the runner's readiness.
lessons.summary: Sprints, middle-distance races, long-distance races and relays place different demands on runners. A sprint requires a controlled start and rapid acceleration. Longer races require a pace the runner can maintain; starting too fast can leave little energy for the finish. Relay teams add baton exchange, timing and commun
lessons.objective: Compare the demands of sprint, distance and relay races and identify safe running practice.

lessons.title: Jumping events
lessons.content:
# Jumping events

## Run-up, take-off and landing

Long jump and triple jump measure distance; high jump measures height. Each event uses an approach, a take-off and a landing, but the technique and rules differ. A long jumper accelerates along a run-up and takes off before the board or line. A high jumper approaches the bar and lands on the prepared landing mat. In triple jump, the sequence of hop, step and jump must remain in order.

## Safety is part of technique

Check that the landing area is level, clear and suitable before anyone begins. Take turns, wait behind the approach line and do not cross the run-up while another learner is jumping. Land in the designated area and leave it promptly when safe. Beginners should practise controlled approaches and balanced landings before trying for distance or height.

Jumping events require a clear approach path, a safe take-off area and a landing surface suited to the event. In a long jump lesson, practise the run-up and take-off separately before combining them; land with control and leave the pit when instructed. For high jump, use equipment and technique only under qualified supervision. Measure from the correct take-off line to the nearest mark made in the landing area. Repeated attempts should include rest, because fatigue can change technique and raise risk.

quiz.question: In a long jump, what makes an attempt a foul at take-off?
options: Taking off beyond the permitted line or board
Landing with both feet
Using a controlled run-up
Waiting for the area to clear

quiz.question: What should a learner do before a jumping attempt?
options: Check that the landing area is clear and wait for a turn
Cross the run-up while another person approaches
Land on an unprepared surface
Begin before instructions are given

lessons.activity: Sketch a long jump approach with the take-off line and landing area labelled; add two checks the class should make before practice.
commonMistakes: A jump is not measured from wherever the jumper lands; event rules define the legal take-off and measurement point.
lessons.summary: Long jump and triple jump measure distance; high jump measures height. Each event uses an approach, a take-off and a landing, but the technique and rules differ. A long jumper accelerates along a run-up and takes off before the board or line. A high jumper approaches the bar and lands on the prepared landing mat. In tr
lessons.objective: Describe the phases of a jump and distinguish the rules and safety needs of jumping events.

lessons.title: Throwing events
lessons.content:
# Throwing events

## Technique and event rules

Shot put, discus and javelin are throwing events, but each implement is held and released differently. A shot is pushed from near the shoulder; it is not thrown like a ball. A discus is released with a controlled turning action, while a javelin is carried and thrown in a marked direction. In competition, the implement must land within the sector and the athlete must follow the event's boundary rules for a legal attempt.

## Control the throwing area

Use only equipment approved for the learner and setting. The teacher controls when the throwing area is active. Throwers wait for a clear signal, aim only into the designated sector and remain behind the line until instructed. No one walks in front of a thrower or retrieves an implement early. Technique is developed with supervision; distance never takes priority over control.

Throwing lessons require strict control of the throwing sector. Only the learner taking a turn should throw, and everyone should retrieve equipment after the teacher's signal. Use age-appropriate implements and begin with light, controlled technique practice. A measured result is taken from the throwing line to the first point of contact, following the event rules. Do not throw toward people or retrieve an implement while another throw is in progress. Stop when the area is unclear or equipment is damaged.

quiz.question: How is a shot put properly released?
options: Pushed from near the shoulder
Kicked toward the sector
Thrown like a small ball from behind the head
Dropped from the boundary

quiz.question: What signals that implements may be retrieved?
options: The teacher or official confirms all throwing has stopped
One learner finishes their own throw
A spectator enters the field
The thrower turns away

lessons.activity: Draw a throwing sector and label the waiting area, thrower's position and safe retrieval route.
commonMistakes: A javelin or discus must never be thrown when people are in or near its landing sector.
lessons.summary: Shot put, discus and javelin are throwing events, but each implement is held and released differently. A shot is pushed from near the shoulder; it is not thrown like a ball. A discus is released with a controlled turning action, while a javelin is carried and thrown in a marked direction. In competition, the implement
lessons.objective: Identify basic differences among throwing events and state the controls needed for safe practice.

lessons.title: Football skills
lessons.content:
# Football skills

## Control before speed

Football combines passing, receiving, dribbling, shooting and defending. A useful pass reaches a teammate in a space they can play, not merely in their direction. Receive with a suitable part of the foot and cushion the ball so it stays close. When dribbling, keep the ball within playing distance and look up often enough to notice teammates and opponents. Defending begins with balance and positioning; charging into a player is not a safe way to win the ball.

## Play within the rules

A team uses the field, goal and restart rules set for the game. Learners should wear suitable footwear, remove unsafe jewellery and check the playing surface. Use a smaller-sided game to give everyone more touches. Communicate with clear calls, share the ball and stop immediately when the teacher signals an injury or unsafe play.

Passing, receiving, dribbling and shooting depend on awareness as well as foot technique. Practise with space between learners, use a suitable ball and look up before passing so that the receiver is ready. A controlled first touch can move the ball into useful space rather than simply stopping it. Small-sided games help learners make decisions, but rules should protect safety and fair participation. Give feedback about one observable action at a time, such as body position or support movement, rather than labelling a learner as naturally talented or untalented.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of cushioning the ball when receiving a pass?
options: Keep the ball close enough to control the next action
Make the ball travel farther away
Avoid looking at the field
Replace communication with teammates

quiz.question: Which is a safe and fair defensive action?
options: Stay balanced and position yourself without charging into an opponent
Push an opponent away from the ball
Trip a player who is moving past
Ignore the teacher's stop signal

lessons.activity: In pairs, practise receiving and returning a pass with both feet. Count controlled returns rather than the hardest kicks.
commonMistakes: A strong kick is not automatically a good pass; direction, control and the receiver's position matter.
lessons.summary: Football combines passing, receiving, dribbling, shooting and defending. A useful pass reaches a teammate in a space they can play, not merely in their direction. Receive with a suitable part of the foot and cushion the ball so it stays close. When dribbling, keep the ball within playing distance and look up often enou
lessons.objective: Explain how basic football techniques and fair play work together during a small-sided game.
