lessons.title: Basketball skills
lessons.content:
# Basketball skills

## Move, pass and control the ball

Dribbling means bouncing the ball with one hand while moving; a player must not carry it or dribble again after gathering it. A chest pass travels directly from the chest toward a teammate, while a bounce pass reaches the floor before the receiver. A jump shot uses coordinated leg and arm action, with the player landing under control. Good decisions matter as much as technique: pass when a teammate has a clearer route to the basket.

## Safe play in a shared space

Keep eyes up while dribbling, give other players room to land and avoid contact that could cause a fall. Use a ball suited to the group and check that the floor is dry. In practice, learners can begin stationary, then add walking and finally defenders. Calling a teammate's name before passing helps them prepare to receive.

Dribbling, passing, shooting and defending are learned through controlled practice and safe movement. Keep the head up while dribbling, pass to a teammate with a clear line and give space during a shot. A defender should move with balance and avoid dangerous contact. Adjust team size and court space so that all players can participate. In a practice game, pause to ask why a pass was available or blocked; this links technique to decision-making. Follow the rules for travelling and contact consistently, and stop play when a learner is injured.

quiz.question: When is a bounce pass useful?
options: When the ball can travel under a defender to a teammate
When the floor is unsafe or slippery
When a teammate is not looking
When the player wants to carry the ball

quiz.question: What should a player do after gathering the ball from a dribble?
options: Pass or shoot without beginning a second dribble
Run while holding it
Start dribbling again immediately
Push through nearby players

lessons.activity: Practise chest and bounce passes in pairs, moving one step farther apart only after ten controlled catches.
commonMistakes: A bounce pass is aimed at a reachable point on the floor, not directly at a teammate's feet.
lessons.summary: Dribbling means bouncing the ball with one hand while moving; a player must not carry it or dribble again after gathering it. A chest pass travels directly from the chest toward a teammate, while a bounce pass reaches the floor before the receiver. A jump shot uses coordinated leg and arm action, with the player landin
lessons.objective: Demonstrate basic basketball control and explain how spacing and communication improve safe play.

lessons.title: Volleyball skills
lessons.content:
# Volleyball skills

## Build a controlled rally

Volleyball teams try to send the ball over the net so it lands in the opponent's court while preventing it from touching their own floor. A forearm pass uses joined hands and a stable platform; the ball contacts the forearms, not the wrists. An overhead set uses the fingertips above the forehead to direct a high ball for an attacker. A serve begins the rally from behind the end line. Teams communicate early so players do not collide while moving toward the same ball.

## Learn with a suitable ball

Start close to the net with a softer ball and a low net if needed. Practise sending the ball to a partner before adding movement or score. Keep fingers relaxed during a set and avoid striking the ball with a closed fist unless the teacher has taught a safe technique. Check the floor and posts before play, and rotate positions according to the agreed rules.

Volleyball uses controlled contacts to send the ball over a net and organise a team attack. Beginners can practise ready position, forearm passing and setting with a light ball before playing at full speed. Call for the ball clearly, maintain safe spacing and avoid reaching across another learner's path. Rotate positions according to the agreed rules so each player experiences different roles. A successful rally depends on communication and preparation, not only a powerful serve. Lowering the net or allowing a bounce can make early practice more accessible while learners develop control.

quiz.question: Which technique is commonly used to direct a high ball to an attacker?
options: An overhead set
A foot trap
A chest pass
A javelin release

quiz.question: Why should volleyball players call for the ball?
options: To coordinate movement and reduce collisions
To stop teammates from moving
To replace the rules of rotation
To make the ball touch the floor

lessons.activity: In groups of three, pass, set and catch a soft ball in sequence; identify the communication that prevents two players reaching at once.
commonMistakes: A forearm pass is made with a stable forearm platform, not by swinging the wrists at the ball.
lessons.summary: Volleyball teams try to send the ball over the net so it lands in the opponent's court while preventing it from touching their own floor. A forearm pass uses joined hands and a stable platform; the ball contacts the forearms, not the wrists. An overhead set uses the fingertips above the forehead to direct a high ball f
lessons.objective: Describe the roles of the forearm pass, set and serve in a volleyball rally.

lessons.title: Gymnastics
lessons.content:
# Gymnastics

## Shape, balance and controlled movement

Gymnastics develops body control through shapes, balances, rolls and linked movements. A stable balance has a clear base of support and controlled posture. A sequence joins movements so that one action prepares for the next. Learners first practise simple shapes close to the floor, where a teacher can check alignment and safe spacing, before attempting more difficult skills.

## Use equipment only as taught

Mats should lie flat, with enough space around them. Remove jewellery, secure loose clothing and wait for a teacher's instruction before using apparatus. Do not copy a difficult movement from a classmate or attempt a headstand, vault or backbend without direct supervision and suitable preparation. A partner may observe a sequence, but should not physically catch or lift another learner unless trained and instructed to do so.

Gymnastics develops balance, body control, strength and movement sequences, but equipment-based skills require a qualified teacher and suitable mats. Begin with shapes and low-level balances on a clear surface, and progress only when control is demonstrated. Never attempt a headstand, lift or partner balance without instruction and spotting arrangements. Learners should wait for equipment to be free and report damaged mats. Assessment should focus on safe technique, effort and improvement, not pressure to perform a skill beyond readiness.

quiz.question: What helps a learner hold a stable balance?
options: A controlled posture and suitable base of support
Rushing into the position
Closing the eyes before learning the skill
Standing on an unstable object

quiz.question: When may a learner attempt a difficult gymnastics skill?
options: After instruction, suitable preparation and direct supervision
Whenever a classmate demonstrates it
On any available surface
Without checking equipment

lessons.activity: Create a three-part floor sequence using a low shape, a controlled balance and a safe transition; have a partner check spacing and stillness.
commonMistakes: A soft mat does not make an unsupervised or unpractised skill safe.
lessons.summary: Gymnastics develops body control through shapes, balances, rolls and linked movements. A stable balance has a clear base of support and controlled posture. A sequence joins movements so that one action prepares for the next. Learners first practise simple shapes close to the floor, where a teacher can check alignment a
lessons.objective: Explain how balance, body shape and safe progression support a basic gymnastics sequence.

lessons.title: Dance and rhythmic movement
lessons.content:
# Dance and rhythmic movement

## Movement organised in time

Dance uses body actions, space, time and energy to express an idea or follow a pattern. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences; tempo is how fast or slowly the beat moves. A movement phrase is a short sequence that can be repeated or varied. Learners can explore clapping, stepping and turning before joining movements into a group pattern. Dance may be traditional, social or newly choreographed, and no single style represents every community.

## Create and perform respectfully

Give each person room to move, agree on a safe direction of travel and use music at a volume that allows instructions to be heard. When learning a cultural dance, ask about its context and use movements respectfully rather than treating a tradition as a costume or joke. A performer can change level, direction or energy while keeping the rhythm of the phrase.

A movement sequence can show rhythm through repeated patterns, changes in level, direction and timing. Count beats aloud or use a steady musical phrase, then practise a short sequence slowly before increasing pace. Provide enough personal space and agree on respectful ways to observe and give feedback. Music and movement traditions may have cultural meaning; introduce them accurately and avoid mocking accents, dress or style. Learners can create different movements to express the same beat, so evaluation should consider control and connection to rhythm rather than demand identical performances.

quiz.question: What does tempo describe in a dance?
options: The speed of the beat
The floor area alone
The clothing worn by performers
The number of spectators

quiz.question: Which choice shows respect when presenting a community dance?
options: Explain its context and avoid mocking its movements
Claim one dance represents every community
Use it as a joke without learning about it
Change its meaning without discussion

lessons.activity: Make an eight-count movement phrase with a partner. Identify its rhythm, one change of level and a respectful way to introduce its context.
commonMistakes: Tempo and rhythm are related but different: tempo is speed, while rhythm is the pattern of beats and silences.
lessons.summary: Dance uses body actions, space, time and energy to express an idea or follow a pattern. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences; tempo is how fast or slowly the beat moves. A movement phrase is a short sequence that can be repeated or varied. Learners can explore clapping, stepping and turning before joining movem
lessons.objective: Use rhythm, space and movement to create a short phrase and describe one element of its structure.

lessons.title: Swimming safety
lessons.content:
# Swimming safety

## Prevention comes before swimming skill

Water can be dangerous even for a confident swimmer. Swim only where a responsible adult or qualified lifeguard is present, in a designated area, and with permission. Never enter water to rescue someone yourself; raise the alarm and get trained help. Do not push others, run on a wet poolside, dive into water of unknown depth or swim during a storm. A life jacket must fit properly and is not a reason to ignore supervision.

## Follow local instructions

Check depth markers, pool rules and weather before entering. Learners who are not confident in water should remain in the shallow area under direct supervision and use approved flotation equipment only as instructed. If someone is in trouble, alert the lifeguard, call for help and follow emergency directions. Swimming lessons should take place with qualified supervision and equipment suited to the learner.

Swimming safety starts before entering the water. Use a supervised facility, follow lifeguard instructions, check depth and conditions, and never swim alone or enter water to rescue someone without training. A learner should tell the instructor about relevant health concerns and use suitable flotation support where directed. Walking, not running, around a wet pool reduces slipping risk. Open water can have currents, sudden depth changes and hidden hazards; confidence in a pool does not make it safe. If someone is in trouble, alert a lifeguard or emergency service immediately.

quiz.question: A person appears to be struggling in water. What should a learner do first?
options: Alert the lifeguard or responsible adult and call for help
Jump in without training
Run away without telling anyone
Wait until the person reaches the edge

quiz.question: Where should a beginner swim?
options: In a designated area with direct qualified supervision
Alone in an unfamiliar river
Beyond the depth marker
Anywhere a flotation toy is available

lessons.activity: Review a pool or water-safety scenario and write the sequence for alerting a responsible adult and getting trained help.
commonMistakes: A learner should not enter water to attempt a rescue; call for trained help and follow the emergency plan.
lessons.summary: Water can be dangerous even for a confident swimmer. Swim only where a responsible adult or qualified lifeguard is present, in a designated area, and with permission. Never enter water to rescue someone yourself; raise the alarm and get trained help. Do not push others, run on a wet poolside, dive into water of unknown
lessons.objective: Identify common water hazards and describe actions that prevent drowning and unsafe rescue attempts.

lessons.title: First aid
lessons.content:
# First aid

## Help while keeping the scene safe

First aid is immediate, temporary help given to someone who is injured or suddenly unwell until appropriate medical care takes over. A learner's first responsibility is safety: do not enter traffic, touch exposed electrical wires or approach a dangerous scene. Call the teacher or another responsible adult, send someone for help and follow the school's emergency plan. Tell the helper what happened, where it happened and what you can see.

## Do not make an injury worse

For a small cut, an adult can help clean it and cover it with a suitable dressing. Do not remove an object stuck in a wound or give food or drink to someone who is unconscious. If a person is unresponsive, having difficulty breathing or bleeding heavily, get emergency help immediately. First aid training matters; a textbook cannot replace supervised practical instruction or professional care.

First aid is immediate help that preserves safety until trained care is available; it does not replace professional diagnosis. First check that the scene is safe, call a responsible adult or emergency service and follow your training. Do not move a person with a suspected serious neck or back injury unless there is immediate danger, and do not give food or drink to someone who is unconscious. For severe bleeding, seek urgent help and use direct pressure only if it is safe and you have been taught how.

quiz.question: What should a learner do before helping at an accident scene?
options: Check for danger and call a responsible adult
Rush into traffic
Move every injured person
Give an unconscious person food

quiz.question: Which information is most useful when calling for help?
options: The location, what happened and visible condition of the person
A guess about the person's medical history
The names of everyone watching
A promise that the injury is harmless

lessons.activity: Use a classroom scenario to practise giving a clear emergency message: location, what happened, hazards and the person's visible condition.
commonMistakes: Do not move a seriously injured person or attempt a procedure beyond your training unless an immediate danger requires it.
lessons.summary: First aid is immediate, temporary help given to someone who is injured or suddenly unwell until appropriate medical care takes over. A learner's first responsibility is safety: do not enter traffic, touch exposed electrical wires or approach a dangerous scene. Call the teacher or another responsible adult, send someone
lessons.objective: Define first aid and choose safe actions for common school emergencies while seeking adult help.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene
lessons.content:
# Personal hygiene

## Everyday habits that protect health

Personal hygiene includes habits that keep the body and shared surroundings clean. Washing hands with soap and clean water before eating and after using the toilet removes many germs. Bathing, wearing clean clothing, caring for teeth and keeping fingernails clean also support comfort and health. Menstrual hygiene is part of ordinary health care; learners should have access to clean materials, privacy and a trusted adult when they need support.

## Hygiene needs water and facilities

Good hygiene is not a reason to shame someone. Clean water, soap, toilets and waste disposal are essential, and not every household has equal access to them. In school, learners can help keep facilities usable by disposing of waste properly and reporting a broken tap or unsafe toilet. Handwashing should cover palms, backs of hands, between fingers and fingertips, then hands should be rinsed and dried with a clean method.

Hygiene routines reduce the spread of some infections when practised consistently. Washing hands with soap and clean water is especially important after using a toilet and before handling food. Keep personal towels and grooming items separate, cover coughs and clean shared equipment according to guidance. Hygiene does not prevent every illness, and a learner who is unwell should tell a responsible adult rather than be blamed. Explain routines respectfully and ensure that facilities, water and supplies are available; advice alone cannot replace access to them.

quiz.question: When is handwashing with soap especially important?
options: Before eating and after using the toilet
Only when hands look dirty
Only at the end of the school term
Instead of cleaning shared facilities

quiz.question: Which statement about hygiene is accurate?
options: Clean water and usable sanitation facilities support healthy habits
Hygiene problems should be used to shame learners
Handwashing is unnecessary when food looks clean
Personal hygiene replaces public sanitation

lessons.activity: Make a handwashing sequence card for the school wash area, including when to wash and what supplies are needed.
commonMistakes: Hygiene education should address habits and access to facilities, not blame or embarrass individuals.
lessons.summary: Personal hygiene includes habits that keep the body and shared surroundings clean. Washing hands with soap and clean water before eating and after using the toilet removes many germs. Bathing, wearing clean clothing, caring for teeth and keeping fingernails clean also support comfort and health. Menstrual hygiene is pa
lessons.objective: Explain key hygiene practices and connect personal habits with clean water and shared facilities.

lessons.title: Nutrition and healthy eating
lessons.content:
# Nutrition and healthy eating

## Food supports growth and activity

Food provides energy and nutrients needed for growth, repair and body functions. Carbohydrates are an important energy source; proteins help build and repair tissues; fats also provide energy and support body functions. Vitamins, minerals, fibre and water are needed in smaller or different amounts but remain important. A varied diet can include familiar local foods such as beans, grains, vegetables, fruit, eggs, fish and safe drinking water.

## Make choices in context

No single food supplies everything the body needs. Meals depend on availability, culture, cost, health and personal needs. A balanced choice combines different food groups over time rather than judging one meal in isolation. Keep food safe by washing produce, cooking thoroughly where needed, using clean utensils and storing food appropriately. Nutrition advice for illness or special needs should come from a qualified health professional, not from classmates or online claims.

A balanced eating pattern includes a range of foods that provide energy, protein, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Needs vary with age, activity, health and access to food, so one menu should not be presented as suitable for everyone. Read labels for serving size and ingredient information, and treat health claims cautiously. Food supports activity and growth, but body size does not reveal a person's diet or character. Discuss affordable, locally available choices without shaming learners or asking them to disclose private household circumstances.

quiz.question: Which nutrient is an important source of energy and is found in foods such as grains?
options: Carbohydrate
Water only
Vitamin C
Fibre only

quiz.question: What makes a meal plan more balanced?
options: Including a variety of food groups over the day
Eating only one favourite food
Avoiding safe local foods
Judging nutrition by colour alone

lessons.activity: Plan a balanced school-day meal using foods available in your community and label the different food groups it includes.
commonMistakes: A healthy diet is not one fixed menu; it depends on varied foods, safety, access and individual needs.
lessons.summary: Food provides energy and nutrients needed for growth, repair and body functions. Carbohydrates are an important energy source; proteins help build and repair tissues; fats also provide energy and support body functions. Vitamins, minerals, fibre and water are needed in smaller or different amounts but remain important.
lessons.objective: Describe the roles of major nutrients and explain why varied, safe food choices matter.

lessons.title: Communicable diseases
lessons.content:
# Communicable diseases

## How infections spread

A communicable disease is caused by an infectious agent that can pass from one person, animal or environment to another. Routes include droplets from coughs and sneezes, contaminated food or water, blood, close contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes. Different diseases spread in different ways, so prevention must match the route. Handwashing helps interrupt some transmission; safe water and food hygiene address others; mosquito nets and removing standing water reduce exposure to certain mosquito-borne infections.

## Respond with care, not stigma

Symptoms alone cannot identify every disease. A person who feels unwell should tell a trusted adult and seek appropriate medical advice. Follow public-health guidance on vaccination, treatment and staying home when advised. Do not share another person's private health information or blame them for becoming ill. Prevention combines individual habits with clean water, sanitation, healthcare access and community action.

Communicable diseases pass through routes such as droplets, contaminated food or water, blood or vectors. Prevention depends on the route: safe water and sanitation can reduce waterborne transmission, while measures against mosquito bites can reduce some vector-borne risks. Vaccination and treatment guidance should come from qualified health authorities. A person who is ill deserves care and privacy, not blame or exclusion based on rumour. In a classroom example, identify the pathogen route and match a prevention step to it rather than assuming one measure controls every disease.

quiz.question: Which action can reduce exposure to mosquito-borne disease?
options: Use an intact insecticide-treated net as directed
Share drinking cups
Leave standing water beside the home
Avoid medical advice

quiz.question: Why should a learner avoid blaming someone who is ill?
options: Illness can have different causes, and stigma does not prevent transmission
Blame is a substitute for treatment
Every disease spreads in the same way
Private health details should be shared widely

lessons.objective: Explain common routes of disease transmission and match prevention measures to those routes.

lessons.title: Non-communicable diseases
lessons.content:
# Non-communicable diseases

## Conditions that do not spread between people

Non-communicable diseases are not passed from person to person through ordinary contact. Examples include some heart diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory conditions and diabetes. Their causes vary: genetics, age, environment, infections in some cases and long-term behaviours can all play a part. It is inaccurate to assume that a person's illness proves they made poor choices. Many conditions have several causes and are affected by access to healthcare and safe environments.

## Prevention and care

Regular physical activity, varied food, avoiding tobacco, clean air and routine health services can reduce some risks, but no habit guarantees that disease will never occur. Early assessment and treatment can help people manage a condition. Learners should rely on qualified health professionals for personal advice, respect privacy and avoid spreading claims that promise a cure without evidence.

Non-communicable diseases are not transmitted from one person to another, although risk can be influenced by several factors including environment, family history and behaviour. Regular activity, balanced food and avoiding tobacco can support health, but they do not guarantee that a person will never become ill. Do not diagnose a classmate from appearance or symptoms. A health concern should be discussed with a caregiver or qualified professional. Public health measures such as accessible screening and safe environments also affect risk beyond individual choices.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a non-communicable disease?
options: It is not passed from person to person through ordinary contact
It is always harmless
It has one identical cause in everyone
It never needs medical care

quiz.question: Which statement about prevention is sound?
options: Healthy habits can reduce some risks but cannot guarantee that illness never occurs
A person with illness must have behaved badly
Screening is the same as treatment
Medical advice is unnecessary

lessons.activity: Sort statements into risk reduction, diagnosis and treatment, then explain why each has a different purpose.
commonMistakes: A non-communicable condition is not contagious, and its presence is not proof of personal failure.
lessons.summary: Non-communicable diseases are not passed from person to person through ordinary contact. Examples include some heart diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory conditions and diabetes. Their causes vary: genetics, age, environment, infections in some cases and long-term behaviours can all play a part. It is inaccurate to a
lessons.objective: Distinguish non-communicable disease from infection and describe realistic prevention and care.

lessons.title: Drug and substance misuse
lessons.content:
# Drug and substance misuse

## Medicines and other substances

A medicine is intended to prevent, diagnose or treat a health problem when used as directed. The same medicine can cause harm when the wrong person takes it, the dose is changed without advice, or it is mixed with other substances. Alcohol, tobacco and some inhaled or street substances can affect judgement, coordination, breathing and long-term health. A substance's legal status does not by itself prove it is safe for every person or use.

## Practise refusal and seek help

Pressure may come from friends, advertising or stress. A learner can refuse clearly, leave the situation and contact a trusted adult. Never take an unknown pill or share prescription medicine. If someone may have taken a harmful substance, do not wait for symptoms to worsen: tell an adult and contact emergency or poison advice services. Do not punish or shame a person who needs urgent help.

Medicines should be used only as directed by a qualified professional or the product instructions, and learners should never share prescription drugs. Alcohol, tobacco and other substances can affect judgement, coordination and health, with risks varying by substance and amount. If someone may have taken a harmful substance, tell a trusted adult and seek urgent medical help; do not wait for symptoms to worsen. Prevention lessons should use accurate information and supportive language. A person experiencing dependence needs professional care, not ridicule or punishment alone.

quiz.question: A friend offers a prescription tablet that was prescribed to them. What is the safest response?
options: Do not take it; use only medicine prescribed or advised for you
Take half to test it
Share it with another friend
Mix it with a drink

quiz.question: Someone may have swallowed an unknown substance. What should a learner do?
options: Tell an adult and seek emergency or poison advice promptly
Wait alone for symptoms
Make the person vomit
Hide the event to avoid trouble

lessons.activity: Write and practise two short refusal responses, then name a trusted adult or service to contact in an emergency.
commonMistakes: Prescription medicine should not be shared, even when another person reports similar symptoms.
lessons.summary: A medicine is intended to prevent, diagnose or treat a health problem when used as directed. The same medicine can cause harm when the wrong person takes it, the dose is changed without advice, or it is mixed with other substances. Alcohol, tobacco and some inhaled or street substances can affect judgement, coordinatio
lessons.objective: Explain how misuse differs from correctly supervised medicine use and identify safe responses to pressure or exposure.

lessons.title: Mental and social wellbeing
lessons.content:
# Mental and social wellbeing

## Health includes feelings and relationships

Mental wellbeing includes how a person thinks, feels, copes with difficulties and relates to other people. It changes over time, just as physical health does. Stress before an examination is common, but persistent sadness, fear, isolation or difficulty functioning deserves attention. Support can include a trusted adult, school counsellor, health worker, supportive routines and connection with friends or family. These supports do not replace professional care when it is needed.

## Listen and respond with respect

People experience distress differently. Listen without teasing, making promises you cannot keep or demanding private details. If someone says they may hurt themselves or another person, tell a responsible adult immediately and stay with them only if it is safe. Protecting a person's safety matters more than keeping a dangerous secret. Seeking help is a practical health choice, not a sign of weakness.

Wellbeing includes emotional, social and physical experiences and can change over time. Sleep, supportive relationships, movement and time for rest may help, but they are not substitutes for professional support when distress is persistent or severe. Listen without pressuring someone to disclose details, keep private information appropriately confidential and tell a trusted adult if there is a safety concern. A class activity should not ask learners to diagnose one another. Respectful communication and belonging can support wellbeing, while bullying and exclusion can undermine it.

quiz.question: A classmate says they may harm themselves. What should you do?
options: Tell a responsible adult immediately
Promise to keep it secret
Tease them to change the subject
Leave them without telling anyone

quiz.question: Which response shows supportive listening?
options: Listen respectfully and help connect the person with trusted support
Demand every private detail
Dismiss the concern as attention-seeking
Guarantee that the problem will disappear

lessons.activity: Create a school support map showing at least two trusted adults or services and how a learner can reach them.
commonMistakes: Telling someone to simply cheer up does not replace listening or connecting them with appropriate support.
lessons.summary: Mental wellbeing includes how a person thinks, feels, copes with difficulties and relates to other people. It changes over time, just as physical health does. Stress before an examination is common, but persistent sadness, fear, isolation or difficulty functioning deserves attention. Support can include a trusted adult
lessons.objective: Recognise signs that someone may need support and identify respectful ways to seek help.

lessons.title: Posture and body mechanics
lessons.content:
# Posture and body mechanics

## Position the body for the task

Posture is how the body is held while sitting, standing or moving. Body mechanics describes how body parts work together during movement and lifting. A balanced stance keeps the feet secure and allows the legs and hips to help with effort. For a light object, bring it close, bend at the hips and knees where comfortable, and rise smoothly rather than twisting under load. Heavy or awkward items should be moved with help or suitable equipment.

## Comfort and movement vary

There is no single rigid posture that is perfect for every person or every task. Changing position, taking movement breaks and adjusting a chair or work surface can improve comfort. Pain, numbness or ongoing discomfort should be reported to a trusted adult or health professional rather than ignored. Safe technique reduces strain, but it cannot prevent every injury or replace medical care.

Body mechanics concern how posture and movement distribute effort during daily tasks. When lifting a light object, bring it close, bend comfortably and avoid twisting while carrying; ask for help with heavy or awkward loads. A desk and screen should allow a relaxed position, but no single posture must be held rigidly for hours. Changing position and taking movement breaks can reduce discomfort. Persistent pain should be reported to a caregiver or health professional rather than treated through a classroom exercise alone.

quiz.question: When lifting a light object, which action generally reduces unnecessary strain?
options: Keep it close and move smoothly using the legs and hips
Twist while holding it far away
Hold your breath and jerk upward
Lift beyond your capacity alone

quiz.question: What may improve comfort during a long classroom task?
options: Adjust the work position and take movement breaks
Hold one rigid pose for hours
Ignore persistent pain
Use the same setup for every body and task

lessons.activity: Observe how a light object is lifted in class. Identify one safe movement and one adjustment that could make the task more comfortable.
commonMistakes: Good posture is not a single stiff pose; comfort, movement and the demands of the task all matter.
lessons.summary: Posture is how the body is held while sitting, standing or moving. Body mechanics describes how body parts work together during movement and lifting. A balanced stance keeps the feet secure and allows the legs and hips to help with effort. For a light object, bring it close, bend at the hips and knees where comfortable
lessons.objective: Describe practical ways posture and body mechanics can reduce avoidable strain during common tasks.

lessons.title: Recreation
lessons.content:
# Recreation

## Leisure with purpose and enjoyment

Recreation is activity chosen during free time for enjoyment, relaxation, social connection or personal development. It may be physical, such as a game or walk, or non-physical, such as music, reading, crafts or community groups. Recreation can help people practise skills and build relationships, but it should remain voluntary and suited to a person's interests and circumstances.

## Make recreation accessible

Safe recreation needs suitable space, equipment, supervision where appropriate and rules that include participants fairly. A school can adapt a game by changing its boundaries, equipment or team size so more learners can take part. Communities may also need to consider cost, transport, disability access and cultural preferences. Recreation is not wasted time, and it need not be competitive to be valuable.

Recreation is chosen for enjoyment, relaxation or social connection and can include games, walking, dance or creative activities. Select an activity that fits the space, weather, available equipment and abilities of participants. Agree on rules and boundaries before beginning, and leave room for people who prefer a lower-intensity option. Recreation can support wellbeing without requiring competition or expensive equipment. After an activity, ask whether everyone could take part and what would make the next session safer or more enjoyable.

quiz.question: Which is an example of recreation?
options: A voluntary community music group
Only a compulsory examination
An unsafe task that cannot be refused
A medical diagnosis

quiz.question: How can a teacher make a game more inclusive?
options: Adapt space, equipment or team size to support participation
Exclude anyone who needs a change
Keep rules unclear
Reward only the strongest learner

lessons.activity: Adapt a familiar game so that learners with different movement abilities can participate, and explain each change.
commonMistakes: Recreation does not have to be competitive or physically intense to provide enjoyment and social value.
lessons.summary: Recreation is activity chosen during free time for enjoyment, relaxation, social connection or personal development. It may be physical, such as a game or walk, or non-physical, such as music, reading, crafts or community groups. Recreation can help people practise skills and build relationships, but it should remain v
lessons.objective: Explain the purposes of recreation and identify ways to make an activity safe and inclusive.

lessons.title: Sportsmanship
lessons.content:
# Sportsmanship

## Compete without losing respect

Sportsmanship is fair, respectful conduct during sport, whether a person wins or loses. It includes following rules, accepting decisions, acknowledging an opponent's good play and taking responsibility for one's own actions. A captain can help by setting a calm example, inviting teammates to contribute and addressing disagreement without insults. Fair play does not mean ignoring unsafe behaviour; a learner should alert the teacher when someone may be injured or at risk.

## Handle disagreement constructively

Players may disagree about a point or rule. Pause, explain what happened briefly and let the official or teacher apply the agreed rule. Do not retaliate, intimidate or blame a teammate for every mistake. After the game, teams can discuss one thing they did well and one action to improve. This keeps competition focused on learning as well as results.

Sportsmanship is shown through actions before, during and after play: following rules, accepting decisions respectfully, encouraging teammates and caring for opponents' safety. A referee's decision can be questioned through the agreed process, but insults or intimidation are not acceptable. Winning does not excuse unfair conduct, and losing does not make effort meaningless. In a reflection, cite a specific action and explain how it affected the game. This makes sportsmanship observable instead of treating it as a vague label for a popular player.

quiz.question: A player disagrees with a referee's call. What is the appropriate response?
options: Stay respectful and let the official apply the agreed rule
Insult the official
Retaliate against an opponent
Stop teammates from following the rules

quiz.question: Which action shows sportsmanship after a loss?
options: Acknowledge the opponents and reflect on what to improve
Blame one teammate publicly
Refuse to follow the closing instructions
Claim the result without evidence

lessons.activity: After a short game, each team names one fair-play action it observed and one disagreement handled appropriately.
commonMistakes: Sportsmanship is not pretending that harmful conduct is acceptable; report unsafe actions to the responsible adult.
lessons.summary: Sportsmanship is fair, respectful conduct during sport, whether a person wins or loses. It includes following rules, accepting decisions, acknowledging an opponent's good play and taking responsibility for one's own actions. A captain can help by setting a calm example, inviting teammates to contribute and addressing d
lessons.objective: Identify respectful and fair actions before, during and after a competitive game.

lessons.title: Rules and officiating
lessons.content:
# Rules and officiating

## Rules make a game understandable

Rules define how play begins, what actions are permitted, how points are scored and how play restarts. They help participants compete on an agreed basis and reduce avoidable conflict. An official observes play, applies the rules consistently and signals decisions so players can respond. In a school game, a teacher may simplify a rule for safety or learning, but the change should be explained to everyone before play begins.

## Practise clear decisions

Officials need to watch the relevant area, learn the signals and remain impartial. Players should stop when instructed, ask a brief question respectfully and continue once the decision is clear. If learners take turns officiating, the class can compare decisions against the written rule rather than personal preference. Consistent application matters more than making a decision that favours one team.

Rules define how an event is played and help participants understand what counts as a valid action. An official applies the rules consistently, watches the play and communicates decisions. Before officiating a class game, learn the key rules, agree on boundaries and explain signals so participants know what to expect. Some school activities use adapted rules for safety or access; tell everyone the adaptation before play. If a decision is uncertain, pause safely and consult the agreed rule rather than inventing a penalty.

quiz.question: What is a central responsibility of an official?
options: Apply the agreed rules consistently
Choose a winner before play
Change rules secretly for one side
Join one team during a decision

quiz.question: A school modifies a rule to make a game safer. What should happen before play?
options: Explain the change to all participants
Tell only one team
Wait until a dispute begins
Leave the change unclear

lessons.activity: Choose one rule from a familiar game, explain it to the class and officiate a short round using the same rule for both teams.
commonMistakes: An official should not change a rule mid-game for one team without explaining a fair change to all participants.
lessons.summary: Rules define how play begins, what actions are permitted, how points are scored and how play restarts. They help participants compete on an agreed basis and reduce avoidable conflict. An official observes play, applies the rules consistently and signals decisions so players can respond. In a school game, a teacher may
lessons.objective: Explain the role of rules and officials and apply a simple game rule consistently.

lessons.title: Injury prevention
lessons.content:
# Injury prevention

## Reduce avoidable risks

Injury prevention begins before activity. Inspect the playing area for holes, sharp objects, standing water and other hazards. Use equipment that fits and is in working order, learn the technique and rules, warm up progressively and match the activity to the learner's readiness. Fatigue can affect control, so breaks and water matter, especially in hot conditions. No preparation can eliminate every risk; the goal is to make sensible choices and respond early when something is wrong.

## Report and respond

Stop if you feel sharp pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or weakness. Tell the teacher instead of hiding an injury to stay in the game. Do not return to activity until a responsible adult has assessed the situation and any medical advice has been followed. Teammates can help prevent injuries by giving one another space, respecting boundaries and stopping when the official signals a hazard.

Injury prevention combines preparation, suitable equipment, safe technique, environmental checks and attention to fatigue. Inspect the playing area for holes or wet patches, secure jewellery and use footwear suited to the surface. Increase training gradually and include rest; doing more when tired can reduce control. A warm-up may prepare movement but cannot eliminate every risk. Report pain promptly, stop the activity when necessary and follow the teacher's or health professional's guidance before returning. Do not pressure an injured learner to continue for the team's benefit.

quiz.question: Which check should happen before a class uses a field?
options: Look for hazards such as holes, sharp objects and slippery areas
Begin at full speed without inspection
Move equipment while others play
Ignore weather and surface conditions

quiz.question: A learner feels sharp pain during practice. What should happen?
options: Stop and tell the teacher
Hide the pain and continue
Ask a teammate to diagnose it
Return to play without assessment

lessons.activity: Inspect a practice area using a hazard checklist and explain which hazards must be removed before play.
commonMistakes: Playing through sharp pain or dizziness can worsen a problem; stop and tell the teacher.
lessons.summary: Injury prevention begins before activity. Inspect the playing area for holes, sharp objects, standing water and other hazards. Use equipment that fits and is in working order, learn the technique and rules, warm up progressively and match the activity to the learner's readiness. Fatigue can affect control, so breaks an
lessons.objective: Recognise preventable activity hazards and describe when to stop and report a possible injury.

lessons.title: Fitness programme project
lessons.content:
# Fitness programme project

## Plan from a clear starting point

A fitness programme should match a person's goal, current ability, available time and health needs. Begin with a baseline that can be observed safely, such as the time spent walking a set route at a comfortable pace. Choose activities that support the goal, schedule recovery and make progress gradually. A programme should include a way to record activity and how the learner felt, not just a target score.

## Review and adjust

At the end of the planned period, compare the new record with the baseline using the same conditions. Consider attendance, effort, enjoyment, rest and any discomfort. If the activity caused pain or was difficult to maintain, revise the plan and seek adult or professional advice as appropriate. Do not use another learner's measurements as your target or promise a particular body shape. The project is successful when the plan is safe, realistic and informed by evidence.

Evaluate a plan by comparing the stated goal with completed sessions and how the learner felt, not by judging body shape. Keep the same simple measure throughout, such as minutes walked at a comfortable pace, and note rest or illness that affected the record. A useful review may find that the schedule was too ambitious or that recovery improved participation. Change one part at a time and set a realistic next goal. If exercise causes persistent pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, stop and tell a responsible adult.

quiz.question: Why should a learner record a baseline before starting a fitness plan?
options: To compare later progress under similar conditions
To diagnose a medical condition
To rank classmates
To guarantee a particular result

quiz.question: Which is the strongest reason to adjust a plan?
options: The activity causes discomfort or cannot be followed safely
A classmate chose a different activity
The plan includes recovery
The record shows realistic progress

lessons.activity: Prepare a one-week activity plan with a goal, manageable sessions, recovery time and a record of how each session felt.
commonMistakes: A good fitness plan is not the hardest possible plan; it is one the learner can follow safely and review honestly.
lessons.summary: A fitness programme should match a person's goal, current ability, available time and health needs. Begin with a baseline that can be observed safely, such as the time spent walking a set route at a comfortable pace. Choose activities that support the goal, schedule recovery and make progress gradually. A programme sho
lessons.objective: Design and evaluate a simple, safe fitness plan using a baseline and progress record.

lessons.title: Science and observation
lessons.content:
# Science and observation

Science and observation is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Science and observation. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Science and observation, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

A scientific observation records what can be detected with the senses or an instrument, while an inference explains what the observation may mean. If a plant bends toward a window, the direction of growth is observed; a response to light is an explanation that can be tested. Ask a focused question, make a prediction and decide what evidence would count against it. Repeat observations where possible and keep the method consistent. A useful science report separates measurements from interpretation and states limits, such as a small sample or changing room conditions.

Keep a dated record and use the same description rules each time. If two explanations fit the observation, design a comparison that could distinguish them instead of choosing the more familiar explanation.

# Laboratory safety

Laboratory safety is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Laboratory safety. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Laboratory safety, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Safety begins with identifying hazards before an activity starts. Wear the protective equipment directed by the teacher, tie back loose clothing, keep food away from chemicals and report spills or breakages immediately. Read labels and never mix unknown substances. When heating, use the correct holder and point containers away from people. Dispose of materials as instructed, then wash hands and return equipment safely. A rule is meaningful when learners understand the hazard it controls; if an instruction is unclear, stop and ask before continuing.

Before leaving, check that heat sources are off, containers are labelled and the work area is clear. Report an accident or near miss promptly so the class can prevent a repeat.

lessons.title: Measurement
lessons.content:
# Measurement

Measurement is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Measurement. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Measurement, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Measurement compares a quantity with an agreed unit. Choose an instrument suited to the scale: a ruler for length, a balance for mass and a measuring cylinder for liquid volume. Read a scale at eye level, record the unit and use only the precision supported by its markings. Repeat readings to notice variation, but do not discard an unusual value without checking the method. Convert units before calculations; for example, 100 centimetres equal one metre. State whether a value was measured directly or calculated from other measurements.

Estimate one digit beyond the smallest marked division only when the instrument scale permits it. Repeat readings and report a sensible average rather than false precision.

For repeated measurements, keep the same starting point and observer where possible. Record the raw values before calculating a mean so the spread remains visible.

lessons.title: Cells and living things

# Cells and living things

Cells and living things is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Cells and living things. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Cells and living things, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Cells are the basic units of living organisms. Many cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material; plant cells also have a cell wall and may contain chloroplasts. A microscope can show structure, but a drawing should include only what is visible at the stated magnification. Living organisms carry out coordinated life processes, including nutrition, respiration, growth, sensitivity and reproduction. A non-living object can show one feature, such as movement, without being alive. Use several observations together when classifying a specimen and distinguish living material from something that was once alive.

A microscope's magnification does not add detail that the lens cannot resolve. Compare the scale bar or field of view when estimating the size of a cell.

lessons.title: Classification
lessons.content:
# Classification

Classification is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Classification. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Classification, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Classification groups organisms using shared characteristics so they can be identified and compared. A key uses paired choices based on observable features; follow each choice in order and avoid guessing from habitat alone. Scientific names provide a consistent naming system across languages. Classification can change when new evidence becomes available, so it is a model rather than a permanent ranking of organisms. Record the feature that supports each decision and note when a specimen does not fit the key. Similar appearance does not always mean organisms are closely related.

A good key avoids vague words such as “large” unless a comparison is defined. Use features that remain visible and can be checked by another learner.

If a feature is hidden or damaged, record that limitation and use another reliable characteristic. Do not force a specimen into a category without evidence.

lessons.title: Nutrition
lessons.content:
# Nutrition

Nutrition is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Nutrition. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Nutrition, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

A balanced diet provides energy and materials for growth, repair and normal body functions. Carbohydrates and fats can supply energy, proteins provide amino acids, and vitamins and minerals have particular roles. Fibre supports movement through the gut, while water is needed for transport and chemical reactions. Needs vary with age, activity and health. Food labels help compare products when serving sizes are considered, but no single food provides everything. Discuss nutrition without shaming food choices, since affordability, culture and availability influence what people can eat.

A meal's nutritional value depends on the whole pattern over time. Health advice should come from qualified sources and account for allergies or medical needs.

For a class comparison, use fictional meal examples and avoid collecting private health details. Explain the nutrient role instead of judging a person's food.

lessons.title: Human body systems
lessons.content:
# Human body systems

Human body systems is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Human body systems. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Human body systems, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Body systems work together rather than acting independently. The digestive system breaks food into absorbable molecules, the circulatory system transports materials, and the respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide. The skeletal and muscular systems support movement, while the nervous system coordinates responses. A flow diagram can trace oxygen from the lungs to a working muscle and carbon dioxide back to the lungs. Identify each organ's role and show how the systems connect. This helps explain why a change in one system can affect the body's overall function.

During exercise, several systems respond together: breathing and heart rate can increase to deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. Explain the link rather than listing changes separately.

lessons.title: Reproduction
lessons.content:
# Reproduction

Reproduction is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Reproduction. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Reproduction, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Reproduction produces new organisms and passes hereditary information to offspring. In flowering plants, pollen carries male reproductive cells to a stigma; fertilisation occurs later when nuclei fuse in an ovule. In humans, specialised reproductive cells join during fertilisation. These processes have different structures and should not be confused. Use labelled diagrams and accurate vocabulary, and discuss human development respectfully without asking classmates to share private experiences. Reproduction supports continuation of a species, while variation among offspring can arise through the combination of genetic material.

In flowering plants, pollen transfer and fertilisation are separate events; in humans, fertilisation and implantation are also distinct. Correct sequence prevents common misconceptions.

A labelled sequence can distinguish pollination, fertilisation and seed development. Each term names a different event, so order is important.

# Matter and particles

Matter and particles is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Matter has mass and occupies space. The particle model explains differences among solids, liquids and gases: particles in solids vibrate around fixed positions, particles in liquids move past one another, and gas particles move freely with larger spaces between them. Heating changes particle motion and may cause a change of state. The particles themselves do not disappear when a substance melts or evaporates. Use a simple diagram to show spacing and movement, and remember that particle drawings are models rather than pictures of particles at their true scale.

Heating usually increases particle motion, while cooling reduces it. During a phase change, energy changes particle arrangement even when the thermometer reading stays steady.

# Elements and compounds

Elements and compounds is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Elements and compounds. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Elements and compounds, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

An element contains one type of atom; a compound contains atoms of different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. A mixture contains substances together without chemical bonding, so its composition can vary. Symbols and formulae communicate composition compactly: H2O represents water with two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. Separate a formula's subscripts from coefficients, which count how many particles are present. Use these distinctions to classify materials and predict whether physical separation or a chemical process is needed.

A compound's composition is fixed, but a mixture's proportions can vary. This difference helps decide whether a material can be separated physically.

A chemical change can form a compound, but simply mixing two elements does not guarantee a reaction. Evidence is needed to show a new substance formed.

# Mixtures and separation

Mixtures and separation is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

A mixture can often be separated using differences in physical properties. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; evaporation can recover a dissolved solid; distillation can collect a solvent or separate liquids with different boiling points. Chromatography separates dissolved substances according to how they travel through a material. Choose a method based on the mixture and the component to be recovered. Label samples, use suitable apparatus and explain which property makes the method work. A clear liquid may still contain dissolved substances and is not necessarily pure.

Choose the collection point before starting: decide whether the goal is the liquid, a dissolved solid or a separated colour. This determines the suitable apparatus.

# Physical and chemical changes

Physical and chemical changes is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Physical and chemical changes. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Physical and chemical changes, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

In a physical change, a substance changes form or state but remains the same substance; melting ice still consists of water molecules. In a chemical change, atoms rearrange to form different substances, such as magnesium reacting with oxygen. Colour change, gas formation or a temperature change may be evidence, but context matters: bubbles from boiling are not proof of a reaction. Describe what was observed, then explain which evidence supports the classification. Mass is conserved in a closed system because atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed.

Reversibility can be a clue, but it is not a complete test. Use evidence about the substances before and after the change to support the classification.

# Force and motion

Force and motion is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Investigation: formulate a question about Force and motion, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

A force is a push or pull that can change motion or shape. Forces are measured in newtons and have direction. Balanced forces produce no change in velocity, while an unbalanced resultant force causes acceleration. Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces, and gravity attracts objects toward Earth. Draw arrows on a simple force diagram and label each interaction acting on the chosen object. Do not confuse speed, which has magnitude only, with velocity, which includes direction. Describe motion relative to a stated reference point.

When several forces act, draw them on one object and combine directions to find the resultant. A stationary object may still have forces acting on it.

# Work, energy and power

Work, energy and power is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Work, energy and power. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Work, energy and power, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Energy can be transferred between stores, including chemical, kinetic, thermal and gravitational stores. Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction; lifting a book transfers energy to its gravitational store. Power describes the rate of energy transfer. A machine may change the size or direction of a force but cannot create energy; some input is transferred to less useful forms such as heating. Identify the system and trace the transfer pathway before describing efficiency. This helps explain why a device needs energy even when it makes a task easier.

For a useful calculation, show the relationship, substitute values with units and check that the final unit matches the quantity being asked for.

# Heat transfer

Heat transfer is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Heat transfer. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Heat transfer, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Thermal energy can transfer by conduction, convection and radiation. Conduction is especially effective in many solids as particles and free electrons transfer energy; convection occurs when warmer, less dense fluid moves and cooler fluid replaces it; radiation can travel through a vacuum. Insulating materials slow some transfer pathways, while shiny surfaces reflect more thermal radiation than dark surfaces. Identify the material and direction of energy flow when explaining an example. Temperature measures how hot a body is; heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference.

A thermos slows energy transfer through its walls and opening, but no container stops transfer completely. Compare designs by the pathways they reduce.

A metal spoon warms by conduction from hot liquid, while moving warm air transfers energy by convection. Identify the material and moving fluid.

# Electricity

Electricity is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Electricity. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Electricity, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge in a circuit. A complete conducting path is needed for current, and a cell provides a potential difference that transfers energy to components. In a series circuit, the same current passes through each component; adding components can change the total resistance and current. Draw standard symbols clearly and place an ammeter in series. A circuit diagram represents connections, not necessarily the physical shape of the wires. Follow teacher instructions and never experiment with mains electricity.

A switch opens or closes a circuit path; it does not supply energy. Check the cell orientation and connections when a bulb fails to light.

In a parallel circuit, each branch has a complete path across the source. A break in one branch does not always stop current elsewhere.

# Magnetism

Magnetism is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Investigation: formulate a question about Magnetism, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

A magnet produces a field in the region where magnetic materials or other magnets experience a force. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Field lines are drawn from north to south outside a bar magnet and are closer together where the field is stronger. Iron filings or a compass can help reveal a pattern, but handle magnets carefully and keep them away from devices that may be affected. A magnetic field model explains forces at a distance without requiring the magnets to touch.

A compass needle aligns with the local magnetic field. Move it around a magnet and mark direction at several points to build a more reliable field map.

A magnetic material can be attracted to a magnet without itself being a permanent magnet. Test whether it retains magnetism after the field is removed.

# Light and sound

Light and sound is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Light and sound. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Light and sound, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Light and sound transfer energy in different ways. Light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum; sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Reflection changes a wave's direction at a surface, while sound pitch relates to frequency and loudness relates to amplitude. Shadows form when an opaque object blocks light travelling from a source. Use ray or wave diagrams with labelled directions. Distinguish the motion of particles in a sound wave from the direction the wave carries energy.

A shadow's size changes with the positions of the source, object and screen. For sound, a vibrating source must transfer energy through air or another medium.

# Weather and climate

Weather and climate is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Weather and climate. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Weather and climate, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions such as temperature, wind, cloud and rainfall. Climate describes patterns averaged over many years. A daily observation cannot establish a climate trend; long records and consistent measurement are needed. A weather station may record temperature in shade, rainfall in a gauge and wind direction with an appropriate instrument. Compare locations and dates carefully, and state the time scale. Climate influences water, farming and ecosystems, while human activities can affect atmospheric composition and local conditions.

Weather data should include the time and place of observation. Comparing measurements gathered with different instruments can create apparent differences that are not real.

Use a series of observations for a climate comparison and note missing days. A short gap can distort averages if unusual weather occurred.

# Water cycle

Water cycle is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Water cycle. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Water cycle, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

The water cycle moves water among the atmosphere, land, oceans and living things. Evaporation and transpiration transfer water vapour to the air; condensation forms droplets or clouds; precipitation returns water to Earth's surface. Runoff, infiltration and groundwater movement affect where water is stored. The cycle is continuous, but local availability changes with season, land use and demand. Label a diagram with process names and arrows, then explain how vegetation or paved surfaces can change runoff and infiltration.

Water can infiltrate soil and later reach streams as groundwater. Paving a surface can reduce infiltration and increase rapid runoff after rainfall.

Plants return water vapour through transpiration, and this process links vegetation to the atmosphere. It is not the same as evaporation from open water.

lessons.content:
# Soil

Soil is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Soil. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Soil, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

Soil contains mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms. Texture depends on the proportions of sand, silt and clay; these affect drainage and nutrient retention. A soil sample should be taken from a defined place and depth, avoiding unusual spots unless they are the focus of study. Compare samples using the same method and record moisture conditions. Soil supports plant growth and habitats, but erosion can remove fertile topsoil. Vegetation cover and careful land use can reduce erosion, although the best method depends on the slope and local conditions.

A simple jar test can separate particle layers over time, but the result is an estimate. A laboratory test is needed for precise nutrient or pH advice.

lessons.content:
# Ecosystems

Ecosystems is best learned by linking observations to scientific concepts. Define the central process or structure, identify its observable features and explain the cause-and-effect relationship involved.

Worked example: consider a familiar laboratory, household or biological situation involving Ecosystems. State what would be observed, explain it using the concept and identify one variable that could change the result.

Investigation: formulate a question about Ecosystems, predict an outcome, identify the variable to change and the evidence that would support or reject the prediction.

An ecosystem includes organisms interacting with one another and with non-living factors such as light, water and soil. A habitat is the place an organism lives; a population is one species in an area; a community includes different populations. Producers capture energy, and consumers obtain it by feeding. A change in one population can affect others through food relationships or competition. Use a food web to trace possible effects and state assumptions, since ecosystems contain many linked pathways rather than one simple chain.

A food web shows feeding relationships, but it does not predict every population change by itself. Consider other food sources, competition and environmental conditions.

A change to habitat can affect food, shelter and breeding sites at once. Explain which factor is most relevant to the organism being studied.
