lessons.title: Corruption and its effects
lessons.content:
# Corruption and its effects

Corruption is the misuse of entrusted power for private benefit. It can include bribery, embezzlement, fraud, favouritism and demanding an unofficial payment for a public service. Corruption weakens trust, diverts resources from intended purposes and can make access depend on personal connections rather than fair rules.

Preventing corruption requires clear procedures, transparent records, independent oversight and safe ways to report concerns. An accusation should be supported by evidence and handled through lawful processes; public rumours can harm innocent people. Learners can identify everyday safeguards, such as receipts for payments and published criteria for selecting beneficiaries. No single action solves corruption, but institutions and citizens can reduce opportunities for misuse and insist on accountability.

A worker asked to pay an unofficial fee for a public service should keep any relevant documentation and use the authorised reporting channel rather than spreading an unsupported accusation. Corruption can divert public funds, weaken trust and make access depend on connections instead of fair rules. Preventive measures include clear fees, receipts, transparent selection criteria and independent oversight. Examine both evidence and process; popularity of a rumour does not establish guilt.

Prevention depends on systems as well as individual choices. Published fees, numbered receipts, clear procurement criteria and independent checks make improper demands easier to detect. Report suspected misconduct through a protected channel and share only supportable information.

quiz.question: Which situation is an example of corruption?
options: An official demands an unofficial payment to provide a service
A public office publishes its service fees
A citizen submits a lawful complaint
A worker follows a transparent selection rule

quiz.question: How should a suspected corruption case be handled?
options: Preserve relevant evidence and report through a lawful channel
Spread an accusation without checking
Destroy records
Threaten the suspected person

lessons.title: Public service
lessons.content:
# Public service

Public service is work carried out by government institutions and employees to meet public needs under law. It includes areas such as education, health, sanitation, registration and infrastructure. Public servants are expected to act professionally, use resources for authorised purposes and treat service users fairly. Their authority comes with duties, including confidentiality where required and accountability for decisions.

Good public service depends on clear standards, trained staff, adequate resources and ways for users to report problems. A delay may result from poor management, insufficient capacity or a missing document; a learner should seek accurate information before assigning blame. Citizens can use official complaint channels and keep records of requests. Public servants serve the public, not a private interest or political party.

When a permit is delayed, the applicant can check published requirements, keep the application reference and ask the responsible office for a status update. Public servants are expected to apply procedures fairly, use resources for authorised purposes and protect confidential information. Delays can have different causes, so evidence should be gathered before blame is assigned. Users can use official complaint channels, while agencies should explain service standards and respond appropriately.

A service standard gives the public a basis for a specific question, such as how long a complete application should take. Keep reference numbers and dates, ask for reasons through the official process and protect confidential records. The response can then be checked against the agency's stated duty.

quiz.question: Whom should a public servant's decision serve?
options: The public interest within the law
A private favour
Only the official's friends
A party's private finances

quiz.question: What is a sensible response to a delayed public service?
options: Check the official process and use a complaint channel if needed
Offer an unofficial payment
Destroy the application record
Assume the cause without asking

It includes areas such as education, health, sanitation, registration and infrastructure. lessons.title: Community service
lessons.content:
# Community service

Community service is voluntary or organised work that benefits other people or a shared place. Examples include a supervised clean-up, tutoring programme or visit to support older residents. A service project should respond to a need identified with the people affected, not impose help they did not request. Participants should agree on roles, safety arrangements and how resources will be used.

Community service can develop cooperation and civic responsibility, but it does not replace public duties such as providing essential services. Learners should protect privacy, obtain permission before taking photographs and avoid making promises they cannot keep. After an activity, review what changed and ask participants for feedback. The value of service is measured by respectful and useful contribution, not by publicity or the number of images shared online.

Before organising a neighbourhood clean-up, ask residents which area needs attention, obtain permission, plan safe waste handling and arrange where collected rubbish will go. Community service should answer a need identified with the people affected; it should not impose unwanted help or replace essential public services. Afterward, seek feedback and review what changed. Protect participants' privacy and get permission before sharing photographs. Useful service is measured by respectful results, not publicity.

quiz.question: What should guide the choice of a community-service activity?
options: A need identified with the people affected
The chance to post photographs
An assumption that outsiders know best
A desire to replace public services

quiz.question: What should learners consider before sharing project photographs?
options: Permission and the privacy of people shown
Whether the image is dramatic
How to avoid consent
Whether participants can be identified without asking

lessons.title: Environmental responsibility
lessons.content:
# Environmental responsibility

Environmental responsibility is the duty to use shared natural resources carefully and reduce avoidable harm. People depend on clean water, air, soil and healthy ecosystems. Everyday choices such as waste disposal matter, while businesses and public authorities also shape pollution, land use and access to services. Responsibility must be matched to the power and resources each actor has.

An effective local response begins with evidence: identify the source of a problem, who is affected and which authority or organisation has responsibility. A school clean-up may improve one area but cannot replace reliable waste collection. Learners can reduce waste, report hazards and support fair community rules. They should avoid claims that blame a whole neighbourhood without investigating the conditions and services involved.

A school noticing litter near a drain should identify where waste comes from and which collection service is responsible before choosing a response. A clean-up may help locally, but regular collection and public infrastructure may be needed to prevent recurrence. Environmental responsibility is shared among households, businesses and authorities, according to their roles and capacity. Monitor whether the chosen action reduces waste and avoids shifting the problem elsewhere.

A response should match the source: household sorting will not replace a failed collection service, and a public clean-up will not prevent industrial discharge. Identify responsible actors, agree on a measurable change and revisit the site. This makes action more than a one-day event.

options: The response depends on the cause and the responsible actors
Every waste problem has one identical cause
Evidence is unnecessary
Blaming residents is enough

options: No; household actions and public services have different roles
Yes; public services are never needed
Yes; only schools create waste
No; individual choices never matter

lessons.title: Digital citizenship
lessons.content:
# Digital citizenship

Digital citizenship is responsible participation in online spaces. It includes protecting personal information, checking claims before sharing, respecting other users and understanding that online actions can have lasting effects. A strong password and privacy settings help, but no setting removes every risk. Learners should avoid posting addresses, passwords, private images or another person's information without consent.

Digital communication can support learning and civic discussion, but it can also spread misinformation and harassment quickly. Check who created a message, when it was published and what evidence supports it. If cyberbullying or a safety threat occurs, save relevant evidence and tell a trusted adult or platform moderator; do not retaliate by publishing private information. Digital rights and responsibilities apply alongside ordinary laws and school policies.

Before posting a class photograph, consider whose faces, uniforms, location or private details are visible and obtain appropriate permission. Digital citizenship includes privacy, consent, respectful communication and checking information before sharing. Privacy settings reduce exposure but cannot prevent screenshots or onward sharing. If harassment occurs, preserve relevant evidence, report through the platform and tell a trusted adult instead of retaliating with personal information.

A reliable digital record includes context: note the original publisher and date, and do not edit an image in a way that changes its meaning. Report harmful content and seek adult support when safety is involved. Do not forward private messages to retaliate.

options: The source, date and supporting evidence
How many friends already shared it
Whether the headline is alarming
Whether it confirms a personal preference

options: Save relevant evidence and seek trusted adult or platform support
Publish the other person's private details
Send threats in return
Delete all evidence and tell nobody

lessons.title: Patriotism
lessons.content:
# Patriotism

Patriotism is attachment to one's country and a willingness to contribute to its wellbeing. It can be expressed through learning about the country, respecting fellow citizens, serving the community and protecting public resources. Patriotism is not the same as supporting every policy or official; citizens can criticise decisions because they care about how public power is used.

Responsible patriotism respects the country's diversity and constitutional principles. It does not justify hostility toward other nations or discrimination against people who disagree. Learners can assess patriotic claims by asking whether an action serves the public good and respects rights. Care for a country includes acknowledging problems honestly and working through lawful, constructive ways to improve conditions.

A citizen who reports damaged public property through an official channel can be acting patriotically by helping protect a shared resource. Patriotism can include service, respect for fellow citizens and honest criticism of policy. It does not require agreement with every official or hostility toward other countries. Evaluate an action by whether it serves the public interest and respects rights, rather than by slogans or displays alone.

Civic pride can include learning history accurately, caring for shared property and asking institutions to meet their responsibilities. Compare a patriotic claim with its effects on other citizens' rights. Loyalty to a country can coexist with criticism intended to improve public life.

options: Yes; lawful criticism can seek improvement in the public interest
No; patriotism removes all disagreement
Only if the criticism is anonymous
No; citizens cannot question officials

quiz.question: Which action can express responsible patriotism?
options: Protect public property and respect fellow citizens
Discriminate against people with different views
Spread false claims about another country
Treat every public problem as unchangeable

lessons.title: Civic action project
lessons.content:
# Civic action project

A civic action project applies civic knowledge to a shared concern. Begin by defining a problem, checking evidence and consulting the people affected. Identify the institution or group with responsibility, then choose an action within the learners' authority: prepare a petition, hold an information meeting or request a service review. A project should not expose private information or promise a result outside the group's control.

Planning includes a goal, roles, timeline, communication method and safety check. Keep a record of what was done and any response received. At the end, compare the result with the original goal and explain what remains unresolved. A project can be valuable even when a public authority does not immediately agree, because learners practise evidence-based participation and learn how institutions respond.

A class concerned about unsafe crossing near school can count traffic at agreed times, document visibility and consult staff and residents before proposing a crossing guard or signage. Identify the authority responsible, assign roles, set a timeline and keep records of responses. Protect personal information and do not promise a result beyond the class's control. At the end, compare the response with the original goal and describe remaining risks.

A project report should include its question, method, findings, action taken and evidence of the response. State what the group could not measure and avoid claiming one activity solved a wider problem. A follow-up check helps decide whether to continue or revise the work.

quiz.question: What should happen before a civic action project proposes a solution?
options: Define the concern and check evidence with affected people
Publish names of people blamed
Assume the first suggestion is correct
Ignore which institution has responsibility

quiz.question: How should learners evaluate a civic project?
options: Compare outcomes with the goal and note unresolved issues
Count only social-media views

lessons.content:
# Agriculture and national development

The agricultural idea of agriculture and national development should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of agriculture and national development. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For agriculture and national development, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Agriculture contributes to national development by supplying food and raw materials, creating work, supporting trade and earning income for households and businesses. Its effects extend beyond the farm: transporters move produce, processors add value, markets connect sellers with buyers, and banks or extension services help producers plan. Reliable local food production can also reduce dependence on imports, although trade remains important for foods and materials that cannot be produced efficiently in every region. For example, cassava may pass from a grower to a garri processor, a wholesaler and a market trader before reaching a household. Each stage adds work and cost. Development depends not only on harvest size but also on fair prices, storage, roads, soil care and access to useful knowledge.

# Branches of agriculture

The agricultural idea of branches of agriculture should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of branches of agriculture. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

The branches of agriculture are connected but require different knowledge. Crop production concerns establishing and managing plants; animal production covers the care and breeding of livestock; agricultural engineering applies tools, machinery and structures; agricultural economics studies costs, markets and farm decisions; and agricultural extension helps farmers learn and share improved practices. Soil science and forestry also support production and resource management. A mixed farm may grow maize for feed, keep poultry and use crop residues as bedding or compost. This example crosses several branches rather than fitting into one box. Knowing the branches helps a learner identify which specialist, tool or information source could help with a particular farm problem.

lessons.title: Farm planning
lessons.content:
# Farm planning

The agricultural idea of farm planning should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of farm planning. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For farm planning, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

A farm plan turns a production goal into a sequence of workable decisions. Before planting, the farmer considers land area, soil and water, crop variety, season, seed quantity, labour, tools, costs, likely buyers and possible risks. A simple field sketch can show beds, paths, water points and boundaries. If a plot is 20 metres by 10 metres, its area is 200 square metres; row spacing and paths determine how much is actually planted. A plan should include a calendar for land preparation, sowing, weeding and harvesting, as well as a budget and contingency for delayed rain or pests. Review the plan when conditions change. Planning does not guarantee success, but it exposes missing resources before they become costly problems.

lessons.title: Soil formation
lessons.content:
# Soil formation

The agricultural idea of soil formation should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of soil formation. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For soil formation, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Soil forms slowly as parent rock breaks into smaller particles through heat, water, wind and living organisms. Plant roots and burrowing animals help loosen material; decaying leaves and other organic matter add humus. Climate affects how quickly rock weathers and how much material is washed or leached. Slope matters too: water can carry topsoil downhill, while flatter land may retain more material. Over time, layers called horizons develop. The upper topsoil often contains the most organic matter and many roots; lower layers contain more weathered material and parent rock. Digging a small profile at different depths can reveal changes in colour, texture and roots. Because fertile topsoil may take a long time to replace, erosion prevention and careful land use are essential.

lessons.content:
# Soil properties

The agricultural idea of soil properties should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of soil properties. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For soil properties, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Soil properties influence which crops can grow and how water and nutrients behave. Texture describes the relative amounts of sand, silt and clay. Sandy soil drains quickly but may lose nutrients; clay holds water and nutrients but can become poorly drained; loam contains a useful balance for many crops. Structure describes how particles form aggregates, while porosity concerns the spaces that hold air and water. Soil pH affects nutrient availability and is measured with a suitable test. A simple hand test can compare how soil feels when moist, but it cannot replace a proper test. Observe drainage after rain, check for crusting and note the depth of roots. Match crop choice and soil improvement to measured conditions rather than judging soil by colour alone.

lessons.title: Soil sampling and testing
lessons.content:
# Soil sampling and testing

The agricultural idea of soil sampling and testing should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of soil sampling and testing. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For soil sampling and testing, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

A soil test is only useful when the sample represents the field. Divide a large or visibly variable farm into management areas, then collect several small samples in a zigzag pattern from the same depth. Avoid unusual spots such as manure heaps, paths, burned areas or places beside a drain unless that location is the specific subject of the test. Remove surface litter, mix the subsamples in a clean container and place the composite sample in a labelled bag. Record the field, date, depth and recent fertilizer or lime use. A laboratory may test pH and nutrient levels and provide recommendations. Do not mix samples from different fields or depths, because the combined result can conceal a problem. Follow the sampling instructions of the service that will analyse the soil.

lessons.title: Soil fertility
lessons.content:
# Soil fertility

The agricultural idea of soil fertility should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of soil fertility. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For soil fertility, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Soil fertility is the soil's capacity to supply nutrients in forms plants can use. Nitrogen supports leafy growth, phosphorus is important in energy transfer and root development, and potassium supports several plant functions, but crops also need secondary nutrients and trace elements. Organic matter improves soil structure and helps retain water and nutrients. Compost and well-managed manure can add organic matter; fertilizers supply nutrients in specified amounts. Neither should be applied blindly. A soil test, crop need, product label and recommended rate guide the choice. Too much fertilizer can damage plants, waste money or pollute waterways through runoff. Rotate crops, return suitable residues and protect soil from erosion. Fertility management combines nutrient supply with soil health rather than relying on one product.

lessons.content:
# Farm tools

The agricultural idea of farm tools should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of farm tools. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For farm tools, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Farm tools are selected for the job, soil condition and scale of work. A hoe can loosen soil and control small weeds; a cutlass can clear light vegetation; a rake levels soil or gathers debris; a watering can applies water to a small bed. Use each tool as designed and keep its handle, blade and fasteners in safe condition. A blunt or loose tool may require more force and can slip. After work, clean off soil, dry metal parts and store tools where children cannot trip over or handle them unsupervised. Carry sharp tools with the cutting edge controlled and pointed away from people. # Farm safety

The agricultural idea of farm safety should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of farm safety. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For farm safety, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Farm work can involve sharp tools, animals, chemicals, machinery, heat and uneven ground. Before starting, identify hazards, agree on safe movement and keep bystanders away from work areas. Wear suitable footwear and protective clothing; gloves and eye protection are needed for particular tasks, but must be appropriate to the tool or substance. Read pesticide labels, keep chemicals in their original labelled containers and never transfer them to drink bottles. Store chemicals away from food, water and children. Do not operate machinery without training or remove guards. In hot weather, plan breaks, drink safe water and watch for signs of heat illness. Know where first-aid supplies and emergency contacts are kept. Stop work if equipment is damaged or conditions become unsafe, and tell the responsible adult or supervisor.

lessons.content:
# Crop classification

The agricultural idea of crop classification should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of crop classification. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For crop classification, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Crops can be grouped by their use, life cycle or plant family. Cereals such as maize and rice are grown mainly for grain; legumes such as beans and groundnuts produce pods and can contribute nitrogen through root-associated bacteria; roots and tubers include cassava, yam and sweet potato; vegetables and fruits are grown for edible leaves, stems, roots or fruits. Some crops have more than one use. Classification helps farmers plan rotations, storage and marketing. For example, alternating maize with a suitable legume can break some pest cycles and improve soil nitrogen when residues are managed well. A crop's group does not replace checking its exact water, soil, temperature and planting requirements. Use the intended product and growth habit to classify unfamiliar crops, then consult reliable guidance before choosing a production method.

# Seed selection

The agricultural idea of seed selection should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of seed selection. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For seed selection, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Good seed should match the local climate, soil, growing season and intended market. Farmers consider variety, purity, viability, maturity period and resistance to common pests or disease. Certified seed usually comes with information about its identity and quality, while saved seed should be selected from healthy, true-to-type plants and stored dry and safely. A small germination test can estimate viability: place a known number of seeds in a moist medium under suitable conditions and count how many sprout. If 18 of 20 seeds germinate, the observed germination is 90 percent. That result can help adjust the sowing rate, but field conditions may differ from the test. Do not use mouldy, damaged or mixed seed. Keep labels and note the source and date so performance can be compared after harvest.

lessons.title: Planting methods
lessons.content:
# Planting methods

The agricultural idea of planting methods should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of planting methods. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For planting methods, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Planting method depends on the crop, seed size, soil moisture and available equipment. Direct sowing places seed in its final growing position; transplanting raises seedlings in a nursery and moves them later. Broadcasting spreads seed over a surface, while drilling or dibbling places it at planned spacing and depth. Correct depth protects seed and allows the shoot to emerge; planting too deep can exhaust a small seed's reserves, while shallow seed may dry out or be eaten. Spacing reduces competition and allows access for weeding and harvesting. For example, a row plan for maize should follow the recommended spacing for the variety and local conditions rather than a guessed distance. Water after planting when needed, but avoid flooding. Record the date, method and seed source for later comparison.

lessons.content:
# Crop maintenance

The agricultural idea of crop maintenance should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of crop maintenance. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For crop maintenance, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Crop maintenance supports healthy growth after establishment. It can include watering, gap filling, thinning, mulching, staking, weeding, nutrient management and regular inspection. The right action depends on the crop and its growth stage. Thinning removes excess seedlings so remaining plants have enough light, water and nutrients; gap filling replaces failed plants while nearby plants are still young. Mulch can reduce evaporation and suppress weeds, but contaminated or diseased material should not be spread. Water at a time that reduces evaporation and avoid waterlogging roots. Inspect leaves and stems for changes, then identify the cause before applying a treatment. Keep a record of what was done and when. A maintenance plan should balance crop needs, labour and water availability, not follow a calendar blindly when weather or plant condition calls for adjustment.

lessons.content:
# Weeds and weed control

The agricultural idea of weeds and weed control should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of weeds and weed control. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For weeds and weed control, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Weeds compete with crops for light, water, nutrients and space. Some also shelter pests or interfere with harvesting. Control begins with identification and prevention: clean seed, clean tools and well-managed field edges can reduce weed spread. Hand weeding or hoeing is suitable for small areas when the crop can be protected; mulching blocks light from reaching many weed seedlings. Crop rotation and close crop spacing can also suppress some weeds. Herbicides should only be used when appropriate, by trained people following the product label and protective requirements. Spraying the wrong product or applying it in wind can injure crops, people or nearby plants. Remove weeds before they set seed when possible, and dispose of invasive or diseased plants safely. Choose an approach based on weed type, crop stage, field size and environmental risk.

# Pests and diseases

The agricultural idea of pests and diseases should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of pests and diseases. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For pests and diseases, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Crop pests damage plants by feeding, boring or transmitting disease; diseases may be caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses or other organisms. Look for patterns such as holes, discolouration, wilting or unusual growth, and check several plants before deciding what is wrong. Nutrient deficiency, drought and waterlogging can resemble disease, so identification matters. Integrated pest management combines prevention, monitoring, cultural practices, biological control and carefully chosen pesticides when needed. Crop rotation, resistant varieties, clean tools and removal of infected material can reduce risk. If treatment is necessary, use a product labelled for that crop and pest, follow dosage and re-entry instructions, wear required protection and avoid spraying near water or pollinators. Keep a record of symptoms, weather and actions. Treating every symptom with chemicals can waste money and harm beneficial organisms.

# Harvesting and storage

The agricultural idea of harvesting and storage should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of harvesting and storage. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For harvesting and storage, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Harvest at the stage that suits the crop's intended use. Immature produce may have poor flavour or low weight, while overripe produce can soften, split or attract pests. Use clean tools and containers, avoid dropping or bruising produce and keep harvested crops out of direct sun when appropriate. Grain must be dried to a safe moisture level before storage; damp grain can mould or heat. Store products in clean, dry, pest-resistant containers and inspect them regularly. Separate damaged or diseased items so they do not spoil sound produce. For example, drying maize before placing it in a sealed store helps reduce mould risk, but it should be dried and handled safely. Record quantity, date and storage condition. Good post-harvest handling preserves quality and income, though no method removes the need to monitor stored produce.

lessons.title: Livestock classification
lessons.content:
# Livestock classification

The agricultural idea of livestock classification should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of livestock classification. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For livestock classification, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Livestock can be classified by species, use, feeding system or digestive system. Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants with a multi-compartment stomach that supports digestion of fibrous feeds; pigs are monogastric; poultry have a different digestive system and are kept for meat or eggs. Animals may also be grouped as dairy, meat, draft or dual-purpose breeds, but actual performance depends on breed, health, feed and management. Classification helps farmers choose housing, nutrition and breeding practices. For example, a dairy cow needs a routine that supports milk production and udder health, while broilers are managed for efficient meat growth. Do not assume every animal of a named breed has the same output. Identify the production goal and local suitability before choosing stock, and obtain animals from a healthy, reliable source.

lessons.title: Animal housing
lessons.content:
# Animal housing

The agricultural idea of animal housing should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of animal housing. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For animal housing, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Animal housing protects livestock from extreme weather, predators, injury and disease while allowing suitable movement and ventilation. Housing needs differ by species and age. Poultry houses require dry litter, airflow and enough floor space; goat pens need secure fencing and a raised, dry resting area; fish ponds require managed water quality rather than a building. Clean manure and soiled bedding regularly, provide clean water and separate sick animals when advised. Overcrowding raises stress and disease risk, while poor ventilation allows moisture and harmful gases to build up. A housing plan should include drainage, feeding and watering points, safe access for workers and a method for cleaning. Inspect structures for sharp edges, broken wire and leaks. Good housing is not simply shelter; it is part of daily health management and should be adapted to local climate and available materials.

lessons.title: Animal nutrition
lessons.content:
# Animal nutrition

The agricultural idea of animal nutrition should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of animal nutrition. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For animal nutrition, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Animals need energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and clean water in amounts that depend on species, age, body condition and production. Roughage such as pasture supplies fibre for ruminants; concentrates provide denser energy or protein. Poultry and pigs need balanced formulated feeds because their digestive systems and growth targets differ. Feed changes should be gradual to reduce digestive upset. Observe appetite, body condition, growth, egg production or milk output as signs of whether management is working, but seek qualified advice when animals become ill. Store feed dry and protected from rodents, mould and chemicals. Do not feed spoiled or unknown plants. A ration should use safe local ingredients and meet animal requirements rather than rely on one ingredient. Clean water is essential; poor water access can reduce feed intake and production even when feed is adequate.

lessons.content:
# Poultry production

The agricultural idea of poultry production should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of poultry production. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For poultry production, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Poultry production includes raising chickens and other domestic birds for eggs, meat or breeding. A flock needs suitable housing, clean water, balanced feed, appropriate temperature and a vaccination and biosecurity plan guided by local veterinary advice. Broilers are selected for meat production and layers for egg production; their housing and feeding programmes differ. Start with healthy chicks from a reliable source and keep age groups separate where possible. Clean equipment between batches, restrict unnecessary visitors and remove dead birds safely according to local guidance. Record feed use, mortality, egg numbers or weight gain so changes can be noticed early. A sudden drop in feed intake or egg production can signal heat stress, disease or a water problem. Do not treat every problem with medicine without diagnosis; prevention and prompt professional advice protect the flock and consumers.

lessons.title: Fish farming
lessons.content:
# Fish farming

The agricultural idea of fish farming should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of fish farming. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For fish farming, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Fish farming raises fish in ponds, tanks or other managed systems. Success depends on suitable species, clean water, adequate dissolved oxygen, appropriate stocking density and feed. Pond preparation may include repairing leaks, clearing unwanted organisms and checking water conditions before stocking. Fingerlings should be active and similar in size; mixing very different sizes can increase competition or cannibalism in some species. Feed small amounts at regular times and observe whether fish consume it. Uneaten feed decomposes, lowers water quality and wastes money. Check water colour, smell, fish behaviour and water level, and seek technical help if fish gasp at the surface or die unexpectedly. Keep records of stocking, feeding, growth, water changes and harvest. Fish farming is a managed production system, not simply placing fish in water and waiting.

lessons.content:
# Goat and sheep production

The agricultural idea of goat and sheep production should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of goat and sheep production. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For goat and sheep production, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Goats and sheep are ruminants raised for meat, milk, fibre, breeding or a combination of uses. Their management includes choosing healthy stock, providing dry shelter, suitable forage, clean water and routine health care. Goats often browse shrubs and leaves, while sheep generally graze grasses, but feeding varies by breed and available pasture. A balanced diet may need supplements during pregnancy, lactation or rapid growth. Inspect hooves, body condition and signs of parasites, and ask a trained animal-health worker about vaccination and treatment schedules. Keep young animals safe from cold, wet conditions and predators. Record births, parentage, treatments and sales to track flock performance. Avoid buying animals without checking health and origin. Good management improves welfare and productivity while reducing preventable losses.

lessons.title: Farm records
lessons.content:
# Farm records

The agricultural idea of farm records should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of farm records. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For farm records, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Farm records preserve information needed to manage production and money. Useful records include planting dates, seed varieties, fertilizer use, labour, feed, animal health, harvest quantities, sales and expenses. A record is most useful when entries are dated, legible and made consistently. For a crop plot, noting seed quantity, rainfall, weeding dates and harvest weight can help compare varieties or methods in the next season. Separate estimates from measured values and keep receipts where possible. Records can reveal that a field yields less, that feed costs are rising or that a product sells well only at certain times. Protect private financial information and keep copies in a safe place. Records do not make a farm successful by themselves, but they support evidence-based decisions and help farmers explain costs, apply for support or plan future production.

lessons.content:
# Marketing farm products

The agricultural idea of marketing farm products should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of marketing farm products. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For marketing farm products, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Marketing farm products connects producers with buyers. It includes understanding demand, grading quality, packaging, setting prices, choosing a market, transporting goods and communicating availability. A farmer compares the expected selling price with production and marketing costs. Selling at the farm gate may reduce transport work but often offers a different price from selling in a town market. Perishable goods need quick handling and an agreed buyer. Weigh products accurately, use clean packaging and state the variety or grade honestly. Check local market prices across several days because prices can change with supply, season and transport conditions. A cooperative can help farmers bulk produce or negotiate, but members need clear records and agreed rules. Marketing is more than advertising; it includes delivering the right product, in good condition, where and when customers need it.

# Agricultural extension

The agricultural idea of agricultural extension should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of agricultural extension. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For agricultural extension, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Agricultural extension shares practical information between farmers, researchers, advisers and other rural organisations. Extension workers may demonstrate planting methods, explain pest monitoring, discuss animal health or connect farmers with soil testing and markets. Advice should fit local conditions and be clear about evidence and limitations. A demonstration plot can compare two varieties under the same management, but differences in soil or water between plots may affect the result. Farmers contribute local experience and should be able to ask questions or report outcomes. Before adopting a new practice, consider its cost, labour, safety, environmental effect and suitability for the farm. Extension is not simply telling farmers what to do; it is a two-way process that helps adapt useful knowledge and identify problems for further study.

lessons.title: Sustainable agriculture
lessons.content:
# Sustainable agriculture

The agricultural idea of sustainable agriculture should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of sustainable agriculture. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For sustainable agriculture, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

Sustainable agriculture produces food and income while maintaining the soil, water, biodiversity and farm resources needed in the future. Practices may include crop rotation, cover crops, compost, careful water use, integrated pest management and reduced soil disturbance where appropriate. No single practice suits every farm, and the result depends on local soil, climate, labour and markets. For example, rotating a cereal with a legume can interrupt some pest cycles and improve nitrogen availability, but the farmer still needs to manage residues and plan the next crop. Avoid clearing steep slopes without protection, wasting irrigation water or applying chemicals without need. Evaluate sustainability over time by monitoring yield, soil condition, costs and environmental effects. A practice is not sustainable merely because it is traditional or labelled natural; assess its actual outcomes.

lessons.title: Farm enterprise project
lessons.content:
# Farm enterprise project

The agricultural idea of farm enterprise project should be connected to farm practice. Identify the resources, conditions and operations involved, explain why each matters, and consider productivity, safety, cost and environmental effects.

Application: Field activity: observe, draw or safely demonstrate an example of farm enterprise project. Label the important features, record the procedure or conditions, identify one productivity consideration and one environmental or safety consideration.

Common misconception: completing a task is not the same as completing it correctly. For farm enterprise project, quality, safety, sequence and suitability of materials or technique all matter.

A farm enterprise project plans a small production activity from goal to evaluation. Choose a product suited to available land, season, water, skills and likely buyers. Estimate inputs such as seed, feed, tools, labour, transport and packaging. Set a calendar for each operation and identify risks such as pests, price changes, delayed rain or animal illness. Use a notebook to record actual spending, work completed, problems and harvest or sales. At the end, compare the result with the plan: calculate revenue and costs, note unsold or damaged products, and explain why outcomes differed from expectations. A project may be a school garden, a small poultry group or a supervised container crop. Follow safety rules and obtain permission before using land or animals. The report should state what the evidence shows and what should change next time.
