lessons.title: Point of view
lessons.content:
# Point of view

Point of view is the position from which a story is narrated. First-person narration uses “I” and limits knowledge to the speaker's experience. Third-person limited follows one character's perspective; omniscient narration can present the thoughts of several characters. An unreliable narrator may misread events or conceal information.

If a narrator describes a neighbour only through rumours, readers should distinguish the narrator's claims from confirmed facts. Ask what the narrator knows, what they may not know and how the perspective shapes sympathy. A shift in point of view can reveal information or create contrast. Do not confuse the author with a fictional narrator.

First-person narration limits readers to one speaker's account, while third-person narration can remain close to one character or move more broadly. An unreliable narrator may omit, misunderstand or distort events; identify evidence for unreliability instead of using the label as a guess. Compare what the narrator claims with what actions or other voices reveal. Ask how a different viewpoint would alter the reader's knowledge or sympathy. Point of view is a deliberate route into the story, not simply a pronoun choice.

Mark what the narrator knows, suspects and cannot know. This boundary helps explain why readers may share one character's uncertainty or distrust another account.

lessons.title: Theme
lessons.content:
# Theme

Theme is an idea or question developed through a work, not simply its topic. A story may concern migration, while its themes explore belonging, obligation or the cost of ambition. A theme is usually expressed as a complete claim about human experience and is developed through events, images and character choices.

In an original story, two siblings disagree about leaving their village for work. Their choices may develop a theme about opportunity and responsibility without offering one simple answer. Support a theme statement with multiple details from the work. Avoid reducing a complex text to a moral slogan or treating a character's view as the writer's final position.

A theme is an idea developed through a text, not a single word such as “love” or “justice.” Formulate it as a claim, for example, “loyalty can become harmful when it prevents honest judgement.” Find moments that develop or challenge the claim, including evidence that complicates it. A theme may remain unresolved, and characters can express competing views. Quote briefly, explain the language and connect the moment to the whole work. Avoid assuming that a character's opinion is the author's final message.

Test a theme statement against a scene that appears to challenge it. Revising the claim to account for tension usually produces a more accurate interpretation.

lessons.title: Style and tone
lessons.content:
# Style and tone

Style is the writer's characteristic use of language and structure; tone is the attitude conveyed toward a subject or audience. Diction, sentence length, imagery, repetition and punctuation all contribute. A formal tone may use measured syntax, while clipped sentences can create urgency, but effects depend on context.

Compare “The door stood open” with “The door gaped at the empty corridor.” The second phrasing personifies the door and may create unease. Name the specific choice, quote accurately and explain its effect in the passage. Tone can shift, so avoid assigning one adjective to an entire work without evidence.

Style includes choices in diction, sentence pattern, imagery and form; tone is the attitude conveyed by those choices. A plain sentence beside an elaborate description may create contrast, while repeated formal language can sound sincere or satirical depending on context. Identify the exact words that shape tone and consider who is speaking to whom. Do not assign a tone from subject matter alone: a sad event may be narrated with restraint or irony. Explain how a pattern affects the reader and support the interpretation with nearby details.

Compare the passage's tone with a later moment before describing a whole work. A shift may expose irony, emotional distance or a change in the speaker's attitude.

lessons.title: Narrative techniques
lessons.content:
# Narrative techniques

Narrative techniques include dialogue, description, pacing, foreshadowing, flashback, repetition and shifts in focus. Writers use them to control information and shape readers' expectations. Foreshadowing offers a clue before an event; flashback presents an earlier event that changes how the present is understood.

If a story repeatedly mentions a cracked clock before a character misses an important meeting, the detail may establish time pressure rather than predict a literal disaster. Interpret technique in relation to the passage. A technique's name is not an explanation: show what the text does and how that choice affects the reader's understanding.

Narrative techniques include foreshadowing, flashback, suspense, dialogue, repetition and shifts in time. Trace a technique through a particular sequence: what information is withheld, when it is revealed and how that changes expectation. A warning early in a story may create suspense only if later events make it meaningful. Avoid naming a technique without explaining its function. Compare the reader's knowledge at two points and support the comparison with evidence. A technique can create several effects at once, so state the strongest one and acknowledge ambiguity where appropriate.

A useful analysis names the technique, points to its location and explains what the reader knows before and after it. This keeps terminology tied to evidence.

lessons.title: Poetry and poetic voice
lessons.content:
# Poetry and poetic voice

Poetry concentrates language through line breaks, sound, rhythm, imagery and pattern. The poetic voice is the speaker created by the poem; it is not automatically the poet's personal voice. A lyric poem may focus on a single moment, while a narrative poem tells a story, but forms can overlap.

In an original four-line poem about a bus at dawn, repeated hard consonants might echo the engine while a pause at the line break delays the arrival. Read aloud, notice sound and pacing, then examine how those features support meaning. Refer to line numbers or brief quotations and distinguish the speaker's feelings from the writer's biography.

The poetic voice is the speaker constructed by the poem and should not automatically be equated with the poet. Identify who appears to speak, the situation and any change in address or attitude. A shift from “I” to “we” can widen the experience or create a claim of shared identity. Read the poem aloud to notice pauses and emphasis, then connect sound to meaning rather than treating rhythm as decoration. Quote a short phrase and explain how its syntax, image or sound supports an interpretation of the speaker's stance.

Notice whether the speaker addresses a person, an object or an absent audience. The choice of address can shape intimacy, authority or distance.

lessons.title: Imagery
lessons.content:
# Imagery

Imagery is language that appeals to the senses or creates a vivid mental picture. It can be visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory or gustatory. Metaphor and simile can also create imagery by linking unlike things. The effect depends on the associations a comparison invites in context.

An original phrase such as “the generator coughed behind the shop” gives sound and human-like action to a machine. Ask what is being compared, which senses are engaged and how the image changes the mood or understanding. Avoid stopping at “it creates a picture”; explain what the picture suggests and why it matters in the passage.

Imagery uses sensory language to shape an idea or feeling. A description of dust covering a family photograph may suggest neglect, memory or change; the interpretation should be tested against the surrounding passage. Notice whether images recur, transform or contrast. A single image can support more than one reading, so explain why one interpretation fits the pattern of the text. Identify the sensory detail, connect it to the speaker's situation and consider how it affects mood or theme. Avoid translating every image into a fixed symbolic dictionary.

Follow an image if it returns later with a changed meaning. Such development can make a pattern more significant than a single striking description.

lessons.title: Figures of speech
lessons.content:
# Figures of speech

Figures of speech use language beyond literal meaning for emphasis, comparison or effect. A simile compares using “like” or “as”; a metaphor makes a direct comparison; personification gives human qualities to something non-human; irony creates a gap between appearance and meaning. Hyperbole deliberately exaggerates.

In “The town swallowed the road,” personification or metaphor may suggest that development has absorbed the route into the settlement. Identify the figure, interpret the comparison and connect it to the passage. Do not label every striking phrase a metaphor, and do not assume that naming a device proves its effect.

A metaphor describes one thing through another, while a simile signals comparison with words such as “like” or “as”; personification gives human qualities to something non-human. Identify the two ideas being connected and explain what the comparison makes noticeable. In “the city swallowed the road,” the image may suggest scale or danger, depending on context. Do not stop at naming the device. Ask whether it sharpens, complicates or challenges the literal meaning, and support the effect with the passage around it.

Explain the qualities transferred by the comparison and whether the context confirms them. A metaphor may invite admiration while also exposing a limitation.

lessons.title: Sound devices
lessons.content:
# Sound devices

Sound devices organise language through repeated or contrasting sounds. Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds, assonance repeats vowel sounds and onomatopoeia imitates or evokes a sound. Rhyme links similar ending sounds, while consonance repeats consonants within or at the ends of words.

In an original line, “soft sand slid underfoot” repeats the /s/ sound. The effect may suggest quiet movement, but context decides whether that reading is persuasive. Read the line aloud, identify the actual repeated sounds and explain how they contribute to pace, mood or emphasis. Avoid claiming that a sound always has one fixed meaning.

Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds, while assonance repeats vowel sounds and onomatopoeia imitates or evokes sound. These patterns matter when they reinforce pace, mood or emphasis. Read the line aloud and compare the sound pattern with the action or feeling described. Repetition may be deliberate, but not every repeated letter creates a meaningful device. Quote the relevant words, name the sound accurately and explain its effect in context. Sound analysis should complement meaning rather than become a list of labels detached from the poem.

Check the effect by reading the phrase aloud in its sentence. Explain how sound supports pace or emphasis without claiming that every repeated sound has a fixed meaning.

lessons.title: Rhythm and metre
lessons.content:
# Rhythm and metre

Rhythm is the pattern of movement created by stressed and unstressed syllables, pauses and line lengths. Metre is a recurring pattern of stresses. In English poetry, an iamb commonly moves from an unstressed to a stressed syllable; a line may vary from a regular pattern to create emphasis.

Read a poem aloud before marking stresses because natural pronunciation matters. A sudden short line or pause can interrupt a steady rhythm and draw attention to a change in thought. Scansion is a tool, not an end in itself: connect the pattern to the poem's voice or meaning, and allow for variation rather than forcing every line into a perfect scheme.

Rhythm is the movement of stressed and unstressed syllables; metre is a recurring pattern that can be regular or varied. Mark a short passage by speaking it naturally before imposing a formal pattern. A pause or extra syllable may disrupt expectation and reflect hesitation, urgency or emphasis. Do not force every line into a named metre when the evidence is uncertain. Explain what the variation does at that moment and connect it to syntax and meaning. Performance can reveal rhythm, but different readers may stress a line differently.

Scan only a short passage first and mark natural speech stresses. Compare a variation with the surrounding pattern before linking it to a pause or shift in feeling.

lessons.title: Dramatic structure
lessons.content:
# Dramatic structure

Dramatic structure organises action for performance. Acts and scenes establish changes of time or place; exposition introduces circumstances; conflict creates pressure; a climax or turning point changes the direction of events. Some plays use episodic structure or an open ending rather than a single resolution.

In an original one-act play about a community meeting, the arrival of a missing document can shift the conflict from blame to negotiation. Consider what the audience knows at each point, how entrances and exits affect tension and whether the ending resolves the central question. Stage structure should be analysed through both dialogue and the action that can be performed.

A play's structure develops through scenes, entrances, exits, revelations and reversals. Identify the event that changes what a character can do, then trace its consequences in later scenes. A turning point may be small in stage action but large in what the audience learns. Stage directions, pauses and scene changes can carry meaning alongside spoken lines. Compare the audience's knowledge with a character's knowledge to explain dramatic irony or suspense. Support the interpretation with the sequence of events rather than retelling the entire plot.

A turning point can be tested by asking what the characters can do before and after it. This gives a reasoned structural claim instead of a plot label.

lessons.title: Dialogue and stagecraft
lessons.content:
# Dialogue and stagecraft

Dialogue reveals relationships, conflict and information through what characters say and how they say it. Stagecraft includes directions for movement, setting, lighting, sound, props and pauses. A pause can communicate hesitation; a character turning away can contradict spoken reassurance.

In a short original exchange, one character says “I am not worried” while repeatedly checking a silent phone. The stage action complicates the line. Analyse speech together with directions and performance possibilities. A script is designed to be heard and seen, so consider how timing, gesture and space shape an audience's interpretation.

Dialogue reveals relationships through what characters say, avoid, repeat or interrupt. Stagecraft includes movement, lighting, sound, props and spatial arrangement, all of which shape performance. A character who speaks while standing apart from a group may be isolated, but the actor's movement and the play's context must support that reading. Select a line and a stage direction, then explain how they work together for an audience. Consider how a production choice could change emphasis without changing the words.

A performance can vary, so separate what the text directs from what a production might choose. Explain how the direction guides, but does not fully determine, an audience's response.

lessons.title: Tragedy and comedy
lessons.content:
# Tragedy and comedy

Tragedy and comedy are dramatic traditions with different conventions, though individual works can mix them. Tragedy often presents serious conflict and consequences, while comedy may use misunderstanding, reversal, wit or reconciliation. A tragic protagonist is not simply a sad character; the structure examines choices, pressures and outcomes.

An original scene can use comic misunderstanding to expose a character's pride, then resolve the conflict through recognition. Another play may end without restoring order. Identify the conventions a work uses and how it adapts them. Genre labels help frame expectations but do not replace close analysis of language, action and ending.

Tragedy and comedy are dramatic traditions with varied conventions, not simple labels for sad or funny moments. A tragic ending may follow from a character's decision, social pressure or circumstances that cannot be controlled; comedy may use misunderstanding, reversal or reconciliation. Track how the work prepares the outcome and whose perspective shapes it. A comic scene can expose serious inequality, and a tragedy can include humour. Explain the effect of the convention in the whole play rather than classifying a scene from one emotion.

Track how the ending follows from earlier choices and pressures. A mixed tone may complicate the genre and make the audience respond with both concern and amusement.

lessons.title: Prose passage analysis
lessons.content:
# Prose passage analysis

Analysing prose means explaining how selected details create meaning, not retelling the passage. Track narrator, setting, character action, diction and structure. A focused paragraph can make a point, give brief textual evidence, explain the evidence and connect it to a larger idea.

In an original passage where a character folds an unopened letter and hides it in a drawer, the action may suggest fear or avoidance. The interpretation should account for surrounding details and remain open to alternatives. Use short quotations accurately, avoid paraphrasing the whole plot and distinguish what the passage states from what you infer.

Begin with a defensible claim about what the passage reveals, then choose details that support it. Analyse diction, sentence structure, imagery, viewpoint and character action only where they contribute to the claim. A short quotation should be introduced and interpreted, not left to speak for itself. Connect the passage to the larger work if the question requires it, while keeping the close reading central. A strong response explains how the writing creates meaning and notes any ambiguity instead of retelling events line by line.

Keep quotations short and interpret their wording. A paragraph should explain how evidence supports the claim, not retell the events surrounding it.

lessons.title: Poetry passage analysis
lessons.content:
# Poetry passage analysis

Poetry analysis considers voice, images, sound, rhythm, lineation and progression of thought. Begin by identifying what changes across the passage: the speaker may move from observation to memory, or from confidence to doubt. Select a few details that support the interpretation rather than listing every device.

For an original poem about rain on a tin roof, repeated sounds may establish a steady rhythm before a final broken line signals interruption. Explain how the sound and line break work together. Quote briefly, refer to line numbers and avoid treating the speaker as the poet without evidence.

Read the whole poem before selecting details so that a phrase is not separated from its development. Track speaker, situation, shifts, images, sound and lineation, then connect them to a clear interpretation. Quote only the words needed and explain their effect. If a poem changes direction at a conjunction or stanza break, show how the shift alters the reader's understanding. Avoid paraphrasing every line or naming devices without analysis. End by explaining how the form and language work together to develop the poem's central tension or idea.

Notice stanza breaks, punctuation and enjambment alongside imagery. Explain how one formal choice changes the pace or emphasis of the speaker's thought.

lessons.title: Drama passage analysis
lessons.content:
# Drama passage analysis

Drama analysis examines spoken language, stage directions, conflict and the audience's position. Ask what each character wants, what prevents them from getting it and how power shifts during the scene. The audience may know something a character does not, creating tension or dramatic irony.

In an original scene, a clerk quietly slides a receipt across a counter while a customer publicly denies receiving it. The prop and gesture may contradict the dialogue. Use evidence from both speech and stage directions, and consider how actors or staging could make the conflict visible. Do not analyse a script as though it were only a narrative.

A drama passage is written for performance, so analyse both speech and stage directions. Identify who is present, what each character wants and what changes during the exchange. Pauses, entrances, props and movement may alter the force of a line. Consider what the audience knows that a character does not, and explain how this creates tension or irony. Use a brief quotation with a nearby direction, then connect the moment to the play's conflict. Do not assume one staging choice is the only possible interpretation.

Compare a character's spoken words with the stage direction at that moment. A mismatch can create dramatic irony or reveal an unspoken response.

lessons.title: Comparative study
lessons.content:
# Comparative study

Comparative study examines similarities and differences between works in relation to a focused question. Choose a basis for comparison such as narrative voice, treatment of power, setting or structure. Compare like with like and support each point with evidence from both texts.

Two original stories may both depict migration, but one may use a first-person narrator who welcomes change while another uses a family dialogue that reveals divided views. Explain how the choices differ and what each enables the reader to see. Avoid writing one full essay about each text with no connection between them; organise paragraphs around comparative claims.

A comparison needs a shared question, not two separate mini-essays. Choose a basis such as voice, power or memory, then examine how each text develops it through form and language. Pair evidence from both works and explain a meaningful similarity or difference. Avoid comparing a whole novel with one isolated line unless the task calls for that scale. Context can clarify different choices, but do not assume one text is superior because it follows a familiar convention. End by stating what the comparison reveals that either text alone would not show.

Arrange paired evidence in the same paragraph and state why the contrast matters. This avoids writing two unrelated descriptions under one heading.

lessons.title: Literary criticism
lessons.content:
# Literary criticism

Literary criticism is reasoned interpretation and evaluation of texts. Different critical approaches may focus on form, history, gender, class, psychology or reader response. A critical lens directs attention to certain questions; it should not predetermine the conclusion or replace evidence from the work.

A historical reading may ask how a text reflects the institutions of its time, while a formal reading may focus on imagery and structure. Both can illuminate a work and both have limits. State the approach, support claims with textual evidence and acknowledge details that complicate the reading. Criticism is an argument to assess, not a list of labels to memorise.

Literary criticism offers a lens for asking questions about a text, such as whose interests a narrative privileges or how class shapes opportunity. A lens is a tool, not a replacement for evidence or a conclusion to impose in advance. Define the critical idea briefly, apply it to a specific passage and test it against details that do not fit. Different approaches may illuminate different features. A balanced response explains what the lens makes visible and what it leaves unexplained, while keeping the text itself in view.

After applying a critical lens, check a detail that resists it. Addressing that counter-evidence makes the reading more precise and less predetermined.

lessons.title: Context and interpretation
lessons.content:
# Context and interpretation

Context includes historical, cultural, linguistic and biographical conditions relevant to a text. It can clarify references and social expectations, but it should not be used to reduce a work to the author's life or the period in which it was written. Textual evidence remains central.

If a poem refers to a public ceremony, contextual knowledge may explain its symbols; close reading still shows how the poet arranges them. Use reliable sources for contextual claims and separate documented facts from speculation. Ask how context changes or deepens an interpretation, and consider whether the text resists a simple explanation.

Context may include a work's historical period, intended audience, publication conditions and cultural references. Use reliable sources and distinguish documented facts from later interpretation. Context can explain why a word or institution mattered, but it does not determine every reader's response. Connect contextual evidence to a specific textual choice, such as a restriction on a character's movement or speech. Avoid treating a community as uniform or assuming that a writer speaks for every person in that period.

Use contextual facts to clarify a textual choice, then return to the passage. Avoid treating background information as proof of what every reader must think.

lessons.title: Writing literary responses
lessons.content:
# Writing literary responses

A literary response makes a clear claim about how a text creates meaning. A useful paragraph states a point, supports it with a brief quotation or precise reference, explains the writer's choice and links the explanation to the question. Evidence should be selected, not copied at length.

For a question about isolation, a response might connect a character's repeated refusal to answer the door with the setting and narrative point of view. Explain why those details matter rather than retelling events. Organise the essay around ideas, use present tense for literary discussion and check that every paragraph answers the prompt.

Plan a response around a claim that answers the question, then organise paragraphs by reasons rather than by plot sequence. Integrate short quotations grammatically and analyse specific words. A paragraph can move from claim to evidence to explanation and link back to the argument. Use present tense for literary events unless discussing historical context. Leave time to check that each quotation is accurate, each paragraph advances the thesis and the conclusion synthesises rather than repeats. Clear reasoning matters more than decorative terminology.

Revise topic sentences so each advances the central argument. Remove plot details that do not support the point, and check quotation accuracy before submission.

lessons.title: Exam practice
lessons.content:
# Exam practice

Exam practice develops the habits needed to read a prompt carefully, plan an argument and use evidence under time limits. Identify the command word: “describe” asks for features, “analyse” asks how choices work and “compare” requires linked similarities or differences. Allocate time for planning, writing and checking.

For an unseen passage, read once for situation and again for patterns in language, voice and structure. Annotate only useful details, then form a claim that answers the question. Leave time to check quotation accuracy, paragraph focus and whether the conclusion follows from evidence. Practise with varied passages rather than memorising one model response.

Read the command word and identify the text, passage and scope required. Allocate time for planning, evidence selection and review. For a comparison, build paired points; for close analysis, stay near the supplied language. Support each claim with precise evidence and explain its effect rather than listing devices. If a question allows more than one interpretation, choose one and justify it. After writing, check that the answer addresses every part of the prompt and has not become a plot summary.

Before finishing, compare each paragraph with the command word and the question's scope. Add explanation where evidence is present but its relevance is not yet clear.

lessons.title: Independent literary study
lessons.content:
# Independent literary study

Independent study involves choosing a manageable question about a literary work, locating reliable context and developing an evidence-based interpretation. Keep notes on quotations, page numbers and source details as you read. A research question such as how a setting changes a character's choices is more workable than a question about every theme in a novel.

Compare your reading with at least one critical source, but do not copy its argument as your own. Explain where the source is persuasive and where the text offers another possibility. Respect copyright by quoting only brief passages with attribution. A clear project presents its question, method, textual evidence, interpretation and limitations.

An independent study begins with a focused question that can be answered through close reading. Select a manageable passage or feature, keep notes with page references and distinguish quotation from paraphrase. Consult criticism for context, but evaluate the critic's evidence rather than adopting the conclusion automatically. Revise the question if the material does not support it. A final report should state the method, explain key evidence, consider a counter-reading and acknowledge limits. Record publication details so another reader can locate the sources used.

Keep a research log with the question, source details and useful page references. This makes it easier to verify quotations and distinguish your reading from a critic's.

lessons.title: Meaning and purpose of accounting
lessons.content:
# Meaning and purpose of accounting

Accounting identifies, records, classifies, summarises and communicates financial information. It helps owners assess performance, managers plan cash needs, lenders judge repayment risk and public authorities calculate taxes. Bookkeeping records transactions; accounting also interprets the resulting reports for decisions.

When a shop sells goods for cash, the transaction changes cash and sales income. A receipt provides evidence, and the record should include the date, amount and nature of the sale. Reliable accounting depends on complete source records and consistent rules. It does not guarantee that a business will succeed, but it makes financial choices more informed and allows records to be checked.

A small shop can use a daily sales record to compare cash received with receipts and stock movement. If totals disagree, the owner should investigate the source documents before changing the books. This shows why accounting is a system of evidence, not simply arithmetic. Reports depend on consistent definitions and a clear period. A reader should ask whether the figures are complete, who prepared them and what decision they can support. Accounting can reveal patterns and obligations, but it cannot guarantee future sales or remove the need for judgement.

A manager can then compare sales, costs and cash timing to decide whether to change prices or order stock. Record the basis for the decision so later results can be reviewed.

lessons.title: Users of accounting information
lessons.content:
# Users of accounting information

Users of accounting information have different questions. Owners may ask whether profit is improving; managers need budgets and stock data; banks examine repayment capacity; suppliers may assess whether invoices will be paid; employees may consider business stability; tax authorities check statutory obligations. Financial statements serve several users, while management reports can be prepared for internal decisions.

A lender may focus on cash flow and debt, whereas an owner may compare return on investment. One report cannot answer every question, and users should understand the period, accounting policies and limitations. Information should be relevant, reliable and timely. Identify the user's decision before choosing which figures to analyse.

Suppose a business reports a profit but cannot pay a supplier on time. The owner may investigate cash collection, while the supplier focuses on payment history and the bank reviews cash flow and debt. Each user has a different decision, so one figure cannot answer every question. Identify the user first, then select relevant information and note its period and limitations. Financial statements summarise recorded transactions; they are not a promise that the organisation will remain profitable or liquid.

Ask whether the user needs a past result, a current obligation or an estimate of future cash. Different questions call for different schedules, even when they concern the same organisation.

lessons.title: Accounting concepts
lessons.content:
# Accounting concepts

Accounting concepts guide how transactions are recorded. The business entity concept separates a business's records from the owner's personal spending. The going-concern assumption treats the business as continuing unless evidence suggests otherwise. The accrual basis records income when earned and expenses when incurred, not only when cash changes hands.

If an owner pays a personal electricity bill from the business account, it is drawings rather than a business expense. If rent for December is unpaid at year-end, the expense still belongs to December under accrual accounting. These concepts make statements comparable and prevent cash timing from hiding the real performance of a period.

Consistency allows meaningful comparison across periods, while prudence asks for caution when estimates are uncertain. The business entity concept separates business transactions from the owner's personal spending, and the going-concern assumption supports continued-use measurements unless evidence suggests otherwise. Concepts guide preparation but do not replace accounting standards or professional judgement. When a case appears to involve competing principles, state the facts, identify the relevant concept and explain its effect on recognition or measurement.

Apply the concept to the transaction's date and evidence, and explain any estimate made. Consistency improves comparison, but a justified change in policy should be disclosed rather than concealed.

lessons.title: Accounting equation
lessons.content:
# Accounting equation

The accounting equation is Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Assets are resources controlled by the business; liabilities are obligations to outsiders; capital represents the owner's residual interest. Every transaction keeps the equation balanced because it changes at least two related elements.

If an owner starts a shop with ₦50,000 cash, assets and capital each rise by ₦50,000. Buying shelves for ₦12,000 cash changes the form of assets but not their total. Buying goods on credit for ₦8,000 increases inventory and liabilities by the same amount. After each transaction, check that total assets equal capital plus liabilities.

Every transaction affects at least two elements while preserving assets = liabilities + equity. If the owner contributes cash, assets and equity both rise. If the business buys equipment on credit, assets and liabilities rise. If it pays a creditor, cash and the liability fall by the same amount. Record the date and source document, then check the equation after posting. A balanced equation is an important check, but it does not prove that every transaction was recorded in the right account.

After posting, compare the supporting documents with both affected accounts. If the equation balances but the transaction was classified incorrectly, correct the accounts and retain an explanation of the change.

lessons.title: Double-entry principle
lessons.content:
# Double-entry principle

Double-entry accounting records each transaction in at least two accounts, with total debits equal to total credits. The entries reflect the transaction's effect, not a rule that debit always means increase or credit always means decrease. Asset and expense accounts normally increase by debits; liability, capital and income accounts normally increase by credits.

When a business pays ₦5,000 cash for stationery, debit stationery expense and credit cash. When it sells goods for cash, debit cash and credit sales. Naming the accounts first helps avoid memorising entries without understanding them. The equality of debits and credits is a useful arithmetic check, but it does not prove that the correct accounts were chosen.

Double entry records equal debit and credit amounts in different accounts according to the transaction's effect. A cash sale debits cash and credits sales; a credit purchase debits purchases or inventory and credits the supplier account. The words debit and credit mean left and right sides, not automatically good and bad. Determine the accounts affected before choosing sides, then check that total debits equal total credits. Equality can expose arithmetic errors, although a wrong account may still leave the trial balance equal.

Use a journal narrative to state why each account is debited or credited. This makes the posting easier to review and helps separate a classification error from an arithmetic mistake.

lessons.title: Source documents
lessons.content:
# Source documents

Source documents provide evidence for accounting entries. Invoices record credit sales or purchases, receipts acknowledge payment, credit notes adjust amounts, bank statements list account transactions and cheque counterfoils record payments issued. The document type depends on the transaction and the business's control procedures.

Before recording an entry, check the date, parties, description, amount and authorisation. A supplier invoice for ₦24,000 of goods bought on credit supports a purchases or inventory entry and a payable. Numbering documents and filing them systematically makes later verification easier. An entry without reliable evidence is difficult to audit and may be incorrect or fraudulent.

A source document provides evidence for a transaction: an invoice records a sale or purchase, a receipt confirms payment and a credit note adjusts an amount. Match the document to the date, party, goods and value before posting. Numbering documents and filing them in order makes missing records easier to spot. A document can contain an error, so compare it with delivery records or an agreement when necessary. Protect customer and supplier information, and retain records according to applicable rules.

A supplier invoice should be checked against the order and goods received before payment is approved. This control can reveal duplicate charges, incorrect quantities or goods that never arrived.

lessons.title: Books of original entry
lessons.content:
# Books of original entry

Books of original entry record transactions first, usually grouped by type. The sales day book records credit sales of goods; the purchases day book records credit purchases; the cash book records cash and bank movements; returns books record goods returned. Cash sales are entered in the cash book rather than the sales day book.

If a business sells goods on credit to Amina Stores, the sales invoice is entered in the sales day book and later posted to the customer's account and sales account. Classification at the first entry determines whether later totals are meaningful. Check that the book's purpose matches the transaction and that each entry has a source document.

Books of original entry organise transactions before amounts are posted to ledger accounts. A sales journal records credit sales, while a cash book records cash and bank movements. Each entry needs a date, reference and correct account classification. At the end of a period, totals may be posted to the ledger, with individual customer balances recorded separately where needed. Choose the book based on the transaction rather than entering every event in one list. Reconcile totals with source documents so omissions can be found early.

lessons.title: Cash book
lessons.content:
# Cash book

The cash book records money received and paid through cash and bank. A two-column cash book may include cash and bank columns; a three-column version can also record discounts allowed and received. Receipts are entered on the debit side and payments on the credit side. A contra entry transfers money between cash and bank and is marked in both columns.

If ₦10,000 is deposited from cash into the bank, bank increases and cash decreases; the transaction appears on both sides of the cash book. Balance the columns at the period end and carry down the balances. Compare the bank column with the bank statement, allowing for timing differences and bank-originated entries.

The cash book records receipts and payments through cash or bank and can serve as both a book of original entry and a ledger account. A contra entry transfers value between cash and bank, such as cash deposited into the bank; it affects both columns but is not income or expense. Balance each side at the period end and compare bank activity with the statement. A correct balance depends on complete entries, accurate dates and distinguishing transfers from external transactions.

Compare the closing balance with physical cash or the bank statement as appropriate. Investigate stale cheques and unusual entries promptly instead of carrying them forward without explanation.

lessons.title: Petty cash book
lessons.content:
# Petty cash book

A petty cash book records small, frequent payments such as bus fares, postage or minor stationery. Under the imprest system, the petty cashier receives a fixed float, makes supported payments and is reimbursed for the amount spent so the float returns to its agreed level.

With an imprest of ₦20,000, receipts total ₦13,500 during the week. The reimbursement is ₦13,500, restoring the fund to ₦20,000. Analyse receipts into expense columns so totals can be posted efficiently. A voucher should show the date, purpose, amount and approval. The imprest system makes unexplained shortages easier to identify than an undocumented cash tin.

A petty cash book controls small payments such as local transport or stationery. Under an imprest system, the petty cashier receives a fixed float, records vouchers for each payment and is reimbursed for the amount spent to restore the float. If the float is ₦10,000 and vouchers total ₦7,200, the remaining cash should be ₦2,800 before replenishment. Keep receipts, check the balance and use authorised categories. The system supports accountability but does not remove the need to review unusual or unsupported claims.

A supervisor can count the remaining cash and compare it with the float less approved vouchers. Keep vouchers sequential and investigate a shortage rather than silently replacing it.

lessons.title: Ledger accounts
lessons.content:
# Ledger accounts

Ledger accounts collect entries relating to one asset, liability, income, expense or person's account. Transactions are posted from books of original entry to the relevant ledger accounts. The debit and credit sides record opposite aspects of a transaction; balancing an account shows the net position at a date.

When a customer pays ₦7,000 owed, debit cash and credit the customer's personal account. The customer account now shows a lower receivable. Use dates and cross-references so a reviewer can trace an entry back to its source. A ledger total should agree with the corresponding control account or schedule when the records are complete.

Ledger accounts group transactions by item, customer, supplier, income or expense. Posting transfers information from the original-entry book while preserving its date and reference. For a customer account, a credit sale increases the receivable and a later cash receipt reduces it. Balance an account by comparing its debit and credit totals, then carry the balance forward as required. A ledger helps locate the source of a total, but accuracy depends on correct postings and timely reconciliation with supporting records.

Reconcile customer and supplier balances with their statements, and follow up on items that do not agree. A subsidiary ledger should support, not contradict, the control account total.

lessons.title: Trial balance
lessons.content:
# Trial balance

A trial balance lists ledger balances at a particular date, with debit balances in one column and credit balances in another. If the double entries have been posted and balanced correctly, the column totals should agree. Agreement is a useful arithmetic check, but it does not prove that every transaction is recorded or classified correctly.

An omitted transaction, an error of principle or equal errors on both sides may leave the trial balance balanced. If totals differ, check additions, balance transfers and whether an amount was entered on the wrong side. Once the trial balance is prepared, adjustments such as accruals and depreciation may be needed before final accounts are produced.

A trial balance lists ledger balances to test whether total debits equal total credits at a date. If the totals differ, check additions, posting sides, omitted balances and transfers. Agreement does not reveal every error: a transaction may be omitted entirely, recorded in the wrong account or entered at the same wrong amount on both sides. Use the trial balance as one control, not proof that accounts are error-free. Keep a clear audit trail when correcting a discovered mistake.

If a difference remains, check whether a balance was omitted or entered on the wrong side before using suspense. Keep each correction traceable to the original ledger reference.

lessons.title: Errors and corrections
lessons.content:
# Errors and corrections

Accounting errors include omission, commission, principle, original-entry and compensating errors. Some affect the trial balance; others do not. Posting a purchase of equipment to repairs expense is an error of principle, while entering ₦540 as ₦450 is an error of original entry. The correction should preserve an audit trail rather than erase the original record.

If an amount is posted to the wrong account, identify the intended account, the account actually used and whether the debit-credit total changed. A suspense account may temporarily hold a trial-balance difference, but it is not a permanent solution. Correcting entries should be supported, authorised and explained.

Errors can affect agreement in different ways. A transposition may create a difference divisible by nine, while an error of omission may leave the trial balance balanced. A suspense account can temporarily hold a difference while an error is investigated, but it should not be used to conceal an unexplained balance. Identify the original entry, determine the correct treatment and record a dated journal correction with an explanation. After correction, check the ledger and related statements to confirm that the effect is complete.

A correction should show the incorrect entry, the required entry and the resulting adjustment. This lets a reviewer see the effect on profit and financial position without erasing history.

lessons.title: Bank reconciliation
lessons.content:
# Bank reconciliation

A bank reconciliation explains the difference between the bank balance in the cash book and the balance on the bank statement at the same date. Timing differences include unpresented cheques and deposits not yet credited. Bank charges, direct debits, interest and dishonoured cheques may appear on the statement before the business records them.

First update the cash book for items known from the statement, then reconcile the adjusted cash-book balance to the statement balance using timing differences. For example, an unpresented cheque reduces the cash-book balance but not yet the bank statement. Do not treat every difference as an error; identify its cause and verify it against documents.

Prepare a reconciliation for the same date and distinguish items that update the cash book from timing differences that remain until the bank processes them. Bank fees and direct debits should be entered in the cash book; unpresented cheques are already recorded by the business but not yet shown by the bank. Verify unusual items with statements and payment evidence. A reconciliation that balances is useful, but a recurring delay or unexplained payment may indicate a control problem that deserves further review.

An old outstanding item should be followed up with the payee or bank. Repeated unexplained differences can signal weak controls, duplicate entries or unauthorised activity.

lessons.title: Depreciation
lessons.content:
# Depreciation

Depreciation allocates the depreciable cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. It reflects use, time or obsolescence; it is not a direct measurement of an asset's market value and does not create cash. Under the straight-line method, annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life.

A machine costing ₦120,000 with a residual value of ₦20,000 and a five-year useful life has annual straight-line depreciation of ₦20,000. The entry debits depreciation expense and credits accumulated depreciation. Consistent estimates and disclosure matter because changing useful life or residual value changes reported profit and carrying amount.

Depreciation spreads an asset's depreciable amount over the periods expected to benefit from its use. The method should reflect the pattern of consumption where it can be estimated reliably. Under reducing balance, expense is a fixed percentage of carrying amount; under straight line, it is generally constant each year. Record the asset cost, useful life, residual value and method, then review estimates when circumstances change. Depreciation reduces reported profit and carrying amount, but the expense itself is not a cash payment in that period.

When an asset is sold or retired, remove its cost and accumulated depreciation and record any disposal gain or loss. Keep the calculation separate from the cash proceeds.

lessons.title: Accruals and prepayments
lessons.content:
# Accruals and prepayments

Accruals and prepayments apply the matching principle by recording expenses in the period they relate to. An accrued expense has been incurred but not yet paid; a prepayment has been paid but partly relates to a future period. Income can also be accrued or received in advance.

If annual insurance of ₦12,000 is paid on 1 October and the year ends on 31 December, ₦3,000 is an expense for three months and ₦9,000 is a prepayment for the remaining nine months. An unpaid December electricity bill is an accrued expense. Adjustments prevent cash timing from overstating or understating a period's profit.

At a reporting date, compare cash paid or received with the period in which the service was used or earned. If rent covers six months beyond year-end, the unused portion is a prepayment asset; if electricity was used but the bill has not arrived, record an accrued expense and liability. Reverse or release adjustments in the correct later period to avoid double counting. Keep calculations and contract dates so another person can verify the allocation. Matching improves period comparison but requires reasonable estimates when exact bills are unavailable.

Use invoices, contracts and service dates to support the time allocation. Recheck estimates when the actual amount arrives and adjust the next period without recording the same expense twice.

lessons.title: Inventory valuation
lessons.content:
# Inventory valuation

Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value under common accounting standards. Cost includes purchase and directly attributable costs needed to bring items to their present location and condition. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell.

If goods cost ₦10,000 but can now be sold for ₦9,200 after ₦500 selling costs, net realisable value is ₦8,700, so the inventory is written down to ₦8,700. FIFO and weighted average are common cost formulas; the method affects cost of sales and closing inventory when purchase prices change. State the method and apply it consistently.

Inventory valuation affects both the closing asset and cost of sales, so a change can alter reported profit. Count items carefully, identify damaged or obsolete stock and retain purchase-cost evidence. Apply the chosen cost formula consistently to interchangeable items and compare cost with net realisable value at the reporting date. For example, an item that can only be sold below its cost may require a write-down. Document assumptions and avoid including selling costs as inventory cost. A physical count and valuation review provide different checks and both are necessary.

lessons.title: Final accounts
lessons.content:
# Final accounts

Final accounts summarise a business's performance and financial position for a period. A trading account calculates gross profit from sales and cost of goods sold; an income statement includes other income and expenses to determine profit; a statement of financial position lists assets, liabilities and equity at a date. Adjustments are made before these statements are prepared.

If net sales are ₦180,000 and cost of goods sold is ₦112,000, gross profit is ₦68,000. Deduct operating expenses to find profit for the period. Closing inventory appears in the cost-of-sales calculation and as a current asset. Check cross-references and ensure each balance is classified in the correct statement.

Prepare statements only after checking ledger balances and making supported adjustments for inventory, accruals, prepayments and depreciation. The trading result flows into the income statement, while assets, liabilities and equity appear in the statement of financial position. Cross-reference figures and confirm that the accounting equation remains consistent. Compare the current period with prior information, but explain changes in policy or business conditions before drawing conclusions. Statements summarise historical records and estimates; readers should use notes and context rather than treating one figure as a complete account of performance.

A final review should compare statement totals with the trial balance and confirm that adjustments have been posted once. Explain any material estimate or classification that affects interpretation.

lessons.title: Trading account
lessons.content:
# Trading account

A trading account calculates gross profit or gross loss from buying and selling goods. Net sales equal sales less returns inward. Cost of goods sold is opening inventory plus net purchases and direct costs less closing inventory. Gross profit is net sales minus cost of goods sold.

If opening inventory is ₦20,000, net purchases ₦75,000, carriage inward ₦5,000 and closing inventory ₦18,000, cost of goods sold is ₦82,000. With net sales of ₦110,000, gross profit is ₦28,000. Carriage outward is a selling expense, not a direct cost of bringing goods into the business.

Classify direct costs by whether they bring goods to a saleable condition and location. Carriage inward may be part of cost of goods available for sale, while carriage outward is usually a selling expense. Returns inward reduce sales; returns outward reduce purchases. Show the calculation in order so a reader can trace net sales, cost of goods sold and gross profit. Compare gross profit with sales only when periods and classification methods are consistent. A margin change may reflect price, purchase cost, stock loss or product mix and needs investigation.

Compare the closing stock count with inventory records and investigate shortages or damaged goods. A correct gross-profit calculation still depends on a reliable quantity and valuation.

lessons.title: Profit and loss account
lessons.content:
# Profit and loss account

The profit and loss account, or income statement, starts with gross profit and includes other income and operating expenses to determine net profit or loss. Expenses are matched to the period they help generate income, including adjustments for accruals, prepayments and depreciation.

If gross profit is ₦28,000, commission received is ₦2,000 and expenses total ₦19,500, net profit is ₦10,500. Drawings are not an expense because they are a withdrawal of owner capital. Classify each item before calculating; an arithmetic total cannot correct a wrong classification.

An income statement reports income earned and expenses incurred during a period, not merely cash movements. Classify expenses by their function or nature consistently and include accruals, prepayments and depreciation where relevant. A business can report a profit but still face cash shortages if customers have not paid or loan repayments are due. Compare trends and investigate unusual items rather than assuming that a larger profit always means stronger financial health. Explain the period and measurement basis when presenting results.

A useful analysis compares margins across periods and asks what changed in price, volume or costs. Avoid attributing a change to management decisions without supporting evidence from records.

lessons.title: Balance sheet
lessons.content:
# Balance sheet

A balance sheet, now commonly called a statement of financial position, reports assets, liabilities and equity at a particular date. Current assets are expected to be realised or used in the operating cycle; non-current assets support operations over a longer period. Current and non-current liabilities are classified according to settlement timing and applicable rules.

The accounting equation must hold: assets = equity + liabilities. If a business has assets of ₦240,000 and liabilities of ₦90,000, equity is ₦150,000. The statement describes a position at one date, not profit over a period. Compare it with prior periods and supporting notes to understand changes and measurement policies.

The statement of financial position is a snapshot at a specific date. Classify resources as current or non-current and obligations by expected settlement, applying the relevant reporting rules. Equity is the residual interest after liabilities, not simply the cash invested. Compare dates to identify changes, then use notes to understand measurement, restrictions or contingent obligations. A healthy-looking asset total may include slow-moving inventory or overdue receivables, so examine quality and liquidity as well as size.

Check whether receivables are collectible and liabilities are complete. Classification alone cannot show liquidity; compare due dates and expected cash receipts with obligations.

lessons.title: Manufacturing accounts
lessons.content:
# Manufacturing accounts

A manufacturing account calculates the cost of goods produced during a period. Direct materials, direct labour and direct production expenses form prime cost. Add factory overheads and adjust work in progress to calculate cost of production. Administrative and selling expenses are not factory costs.

If prime cost is ₦80,000, factory overhead is ₦24,000, opening work in progress ₦6,000 and closing work in progress ₦10,000, cost of production is ₦100,000. The closing work in progress is deducted because that production is unfinished. The cost of production is then transferred to the trading account as part of goods available for sale.

A manufacturing account calculates the cost of goods produced by combining direct materials, direct labour and production overheads. Opening work in progress is added and closing work in progress is deducted to find production cost for the period. Distinguish factory costs from selling and administration expenses. If materials issued to production are ₦40,000, direct labour is ₦25,000 and factory overhead is ₦15,000, prime cost is ₦65,000 and factory cost before work-in-progress adjustments is ₦80,000. State classifications and check that units and period match.

Production records should reconcile materials issued, labour time and overhead allocation with output. Explain the basis for shared factory costs so unit costs can be compared fairly.

lessons.title: Partnership accounts
lessons.content:
# Partnership accounts

A partnership is a business owned by two or more partners under an agreed arrangement. The partnership agreement should state capital contributions, profit-sharing ratios, drawings, salaries or interest on capital where applicable. Profit is shared according to the agreement, not automatically in proportion to capital.

If partners share profit 3:2 and the distributable profit is ₦100,000, their shares are ₦60,000 and ₦40,000. A profit appropriation account shows how profit is allocated after any agreed adjustments. Keep partners' capital and current accounts distinct so permanent contributions are not confused with drawings or annual allocations.

A partnership agreement may specify capital contributions, profit-sharing ratios, interest on capital, salaries and interest on drawings. Apply the agreed terms before dividing residual profit; a partner's salary is an appropriation of profit, not necessarily a business operating expense. Record drawings separately from expenses and reconcile each partner's capital or current account. If the agreement is silent, the applicable legal default may matter, so do not assume a customary arrangement. Explain the basis used and check that appropriations do not exceed the profit available.

Show each appropriation separately and verify the agreed ratio before allocating residual profit. Partners should review the statement and resolve differences using the partnership agreement.

lessons.title: Company accounts
lessons.content:
# Company accounts

A company is a separate legal entity from its shareholders. Share capital represents funds contributed for ownership shares; retained earnings are accumulated profits not distributed. A dividend is a distribution to shareholders and is not an operating expense used to calculate profit.

If a company earns profit after tax of ₦500,000 and declares a dividend of ₦120,000, retained earnings increase by the undistributed amount, subject to other movements and legal requirements. Company accounts follow statutory reporting and disclosure rules. Distinguish issued share capital, liabilities and reserves when reading a statement of financial position.

A company is a separate legal entity from its shareholders, so company transactions must not be mixed with owners' personal spending. Share capital represents funds raised by issuing shares, while retained earnings accumulate profits kept in the business after distributions. Dividends are distributions to shareholders, not operating expenses. Read the statement dates and notes, since accounting classifications and legal requirements depend on the applicable framework. A shareholder's investment does not guarantee a dividend, and a profit figure does not alone establish the company's ability to pay one.

Check whether share issues, reserves and distributions are supported by company records and the relevant approvals. Do not treat a shareholder's personal transaction as a company expense.

lessons.title: Cash-flow information
lessons.content:
# Cash-flow information

A cash-flow statement explains cash and cash-equivalent movements during a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities. Profit is not the same as cash flow because credit sales, non-cash expenses and timing differences affect when cash moves.

A credit sale can increase revenue and profit before the customer pays; depreciation reduces profit but does not use cash in that period. Cash-flow information helps assess whether a business can pay suppliers, invest and meet loan obligations. Reconcile the opening cash balance to the closing balance and explain material movements rather than relying on profit alone.

Cash-flow information explains movements in cash over a period and groups them by operating, investing and financing activities. Profit differs from operating cash flow because of non-cash expenses, working-capital changes and timing of receipts or payments. A business can be profitable yet unable to pay a bill when due. Compare cash flow with obligations and planned investment, and check whether a one-off receipt disguises a recurring shortfall. Trace each amount to the underlying statement and avoid counting a transfer between cash accounts as an external cash flow.

Review whether operating cash flow can meet near-term payments and whether capital spending has a sustainable funding source. Explain temporary timing differences separately from recurring shortages.

lessons.title: Accounting ratios
lessons.content:
# Accounting ratios

Accounting ratios compare related figures to assess profitability, liquidity, efficiency or solvency. The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Gross-profit margin is gross profit divided by revenue, multiplied by 100. Ratios are meaningful when calculated consistently and compared with prior periods, plans or relevant organisations.

If current assets are ₦90,000 and current liabilities are ₦45,000, the current ratio is 2:1. This does not by itself prove the business is healthy: inventory may be slow-moving and debts may fall due soon. Read ratios alongside the underlying statements and business context. State the formula, units or percentage and what the result can and cannot show.

Ratios relate financial statement figures to support comparison, but their meaning depends on consistent definitions and context. A current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities; a gross margin compares gross profit with sales. Compare the same business over time and, cautiously, with similar organisations. A high ratio is not automatically good: excess inventory may weaken liquidity, while high margins could coincide with falling sales. State the formula, period and data source, then explain what the result suggests and what it cannot prove.

Use the same formula and period for comparisons, and state when classifications differ. A ratio is a prompt for investigation, not a standalone verdict about management quality.

lessons.title: Computerized accounting
lessons.content:
# Computerized accounting

Computerized accounting uses software to record transactions, post entries and prepare reports. A chart of accounts defines categories; each transaction is entered with a date, amount, account and supporting document. The software can automate calculations, but incorrect input or setup can still produce misleading reports.

Access controls, backups, audit trails and regular reconciliations protect the records. Restrict permissions according to each user's responsibilities, and do not share passwords. Before relying on a report, check the period, account mapping and whether all transactions were entered. Automation improves speed and consistency only when the underlying data and procedures are sound.

Accounting software can automate calculations, organise records and produce reports, but it depends on accurate setup and input. Assign appropriate permissions, use unique user accounts and back up data securely. Reconcile imported bank transactions with statements and review suggested account codes before accepting them. Keep an audit trail for edits and protect customer or payroll information. Automation may reduce repetitive arithmetic errors, but it cannot decide whether a transaction is genuine or correctly classified without human review.

Restrict access by role, preserve audit logs and test backups by restoring a sample. Review unusual automated matches before posting because software can repeat a wrong rule quickly.

lessons.title: Accounting project
lessons.content:
# Accounting project

An accounting project applies recording and analysis to a small, realistic entity. Define the period and scope, obtain permission to use records, and protect personal or commercially sensitive information. Collect source documents, classify transactions, record entries and check that debits equal credits before preparing a trial balance or statements.

Explain the accounting policies and any estimates used, such as depreciation or inventory valuation. Reconcile important balances and note limitations, including missing documents or incomplete periods. Present findings clearly and avoid claiming that a sample proves more than it can. A good project is traceable: a reader can follow each conclusion back to evidence.

A practical project should define a small organisation, period and question before collecting sample transactions. Use realistic source documents, record each event in the correct book, post to ledgers and prepare a trial balance or selected statement. Mark fictional data clearly and do not use real classmates' financial details. Check totals at each stage and include one example of a control or correction. The report should explain the method, findings and limitations so another learner can reproduce the work and identify where an error might arise.

Include enough anonymised source records for a classmate to reproduce one transaction from entry through report. Explain a discrepancy and show how the correction changed the final figures.

lessons.title: Computer as a machine
lessons.content:
# Computer as a machine

A computer is an electronic system that accepts data, processes it according to instructions, stores information and produces output. The input-process-output-storage model helps trace a task. When a learner types marks, the keyboard supplies input, software calculates a total, the screen displays it and a file may store it for later use.

Hardware is the physical equipment; software is the set of programs and instructions. A computer does not understand a result in the human sense: it follows operations encoded by software. The quality of output depends on the accuracy of input and the correctness of the instructions. This is why checking source data matters before relying on a calculation.

Trace a school attendance task through input, processing, output and storage. Name one possible error at each stage.

A computer's result depends on the quality of its input and instructions. In a class attendance example, a misspelled learner name may create a duplicate record, while an incorrect formula may count the wrong range. Check the original register, test the calculation with a small sample and compare the final total with a second method. This is called verification: it looks for errors after processing rather than assuming that a computer is always correct. Computers can repeat instructions quickly, but they do not decide whether the task is fair or whether the data should have been collected. A user remains responsible for checking the purpose, accuracy and appropriate handling of information.

lessons.title: Parts of a computer
lessons.content:
# Parts of a computer

A computer system includes input devices, a processor, memory, storage and output devices. The CPU executes instructions and coordinates operations. RAM temporarily holds data and programs currently in use; it is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is removed. Storage devices such as SSDs keep files when the computer is off.

These parts work together rather than independently. When opening a document, the storage device supplies its data, RAM holds working information, the processor runs the application and the display presents the page. A printer is an output device, while a keyboard supplies input. Knowing each part's role makes troubleshooting more precise than saying simply that “the computer is faulty.”

For printing a saved document, identify which component stores the file, processes the print command and produces the paper output.

The component roles are easiest to remember by tracing one complete task. When editing a saved report, storage supplies the file, RAM holds the open working copy, the CPU executes the editor's instructions and the display shows the current page. Saving sends updated data back to storage. If the printer is offline, the report may still be open because output and processing are separate functions. This distinction helps diagnose a problem: a blank display, a full drive and a disconnected printer point to different components. Identify the symptom first, then check the relevant connection, setting or resource rather than replacing every part of the system.

lessons.title: Input devices
lessons.content:
# Input devices

An input device sends data or instructions to a computer. A keyboard enters text, a mouse controls a pointer, a microphone captures sound and a scanner converts a paper image into digital data. Touchscreens can both show output and detect input. Choose a device according to the kind of information and the task.

Input must be interpreted by software. A barcode scanner reads a code that identifies a product; it does not itself decide the price. A microphone captures an analogue sound signal that the system converts into digital data. Devices need compatible ports, drivers or wireless connections, and the user may need to grant permission before an application can access them.

For recording a spoken interview and then typing its transcript, name the input device used at each stage and the data it captures.

Select an input device by considering the form of data, accuracy required and conditions of use. A barcode reader is efficient for repeated product codes, while a keyboard is better for entering a person's name. A microphone may capture speech, but background noise can reduce recognition accuracy. Before recording people, explain the purpose and obtain appropriate permission; before scanning a document, check that the resulting file is legible. The device transfers a signal, and software interprets it according to a format. If the wrong device or setting is selected, the system may receive incomplete or misleading data. Test the input with a small sample before relying on it for a larger task.

lessons.title: Output devices
lessons.content:
# Output devices

An output device presents processed information in a form people or other systems can use. A monitor displays text and images, speakers produce sound, a printer creates a paper copy and a projector enlarges an image for a group. Output quality depends on the device and on how the software prepares the information.

Different tasks call for different output. A printed receipt is useful when a customer needs a physical record; a screen is better for information that changes frequently. Resolution, colour capability, paper size and accessibility features should be considered when choosing a device. Output can also return to a computer, as when a printer reports that it is out of paper.

Choose an output device for a class presentation and one for a signed payment receipt. Explain why the two tasks differ.

Output should suit both the information and its audience. A chart projected to a classroom needs large labels and strong contrast, while a printed receipt needs a clear date, amount and business identifier. A speaker may communicate an alert to a group, but a person with hearing loss may need a visual message as well. Check the output after it is produced: compare a printed total with the source record and confirm that a presentation is readable from the back of the room. Output devices present results; they do not guarantee that the results are accurate or accessible. Choose more than one form when the audience or task requires it.

lessons.title: Storage devices
lessons.content:
# Storage devices

Storage keeps programs and data for later use. A hard disk and a solid-state drive retain files without power; an SSD has no moving disk parts and is usually faster. A USB flash drive is portable, while cloud storage keeps data on remote systems accessed through a network. RAM is working memory, not permanent storage.

Capacity measures how much data a device can hold; access speed and reliability also matter. A backup is a separate copy that helps recover data after loss or damage. Saving a file to one device is not a complete backup if that device is the only copy. Removable media should be handled safely and scanned when its source is unknown.

Choose storage for a school project that must be edited in class and backed up at home. State one benefit and one risk of your choice.

Choose storage by balancing capacity, speed, portability, durability and access control. A learner may keep an editable working copy on a laptop and a separate backup on approved school storage. If both copies remain on the same device, theft or hardware failure can remove them together. Cloud storage can support access from several locations, but requires a reliable connection and careful account security. Organise versions clearly and test that a backup can actually be opened; an unreadable copy is not useful recovery. Avoid saving private records to a shared public device. A storage plan should state what is kept, where it is backed up and who is allowed to access it.

lessons.title: Data and information
lessons.content:
# Data and information

Data are recorded facts or symbols; information is data organised and interpreted so it answers a question. The marks 62, 74 and 81 are data. A calculated mean of 72.3, labelled as the class average for a named test, is information because it has context and meaning.

Data quality affects information quality. Incorrect spelling, missing values or marks entered in the wrong column can produce misleading reports. Validation checks can detect some errors, such as a score outside the allowed range, but they cannot prove every entry is true. Keep the original source and document how data was collected when decisions depend on it.

Give an example of raw school data and show how adding labels and a calculation turns it into useful information.

Information is useful only when its context is clear. A list of marks without learner names, subject, date or maximum score cannot answer whether a class improved. Before calculating a mean, check that every value belongs to the same assessment and that missing entries are treated consistently. Validation can flag a mark above the maximum, but a plausible number may still have been entered for the wrong learner. Preserve the original record and note any corrections so another person can trace how the report was made. When presenting results, use labels and an explanation that answer a specific question without exposing personal data unnecessarily.
